meta.title: Complete Code Smells Knowledge Base (Code Smells Knowledge Base)
meta.description: Hierarchical database of code smells with clear definitions, symptoms, causes, impact, detection metrics, refactoring techniques, and examples of bad and good code.

categories.name: Bloaters
categories.description: Code, methods, and classes that have grown to such proportions that they are difficult to work with. Usually accumulate gradually as functionality evolves.

subcategories.name: Method Bloat
subcategories.description: Methods with excessive length, complex control flow, or overloaded signatures.

subcategories.name: Class Bloat
subcategories.description: Classes accumulating excessive responsibilities, fields, and behavior.

subcategories.name: Data Bloat
subcategories.description: Inefficient use of basic primitives and clumped parameter groups.

categories.name: Object-Orientation Abusers
categories.description: Erroneous or incomplete application of object-oriented programming principles (encapsulation, polymorphism, inheritance).

subcategories.name: Inheritance Abuse
subcategories.description: Incorrect use of inheritance instead of composition, violation of the Liskov substitution principle.

subcategories.name: Conditional Complexity
subcategories.description: Using switch/if branches instead of polymorphism and design patterns.

subcategories.name: State & Encapsulation Abuse
subcategories.description: Temporary fields, anemic models, and deficient object contracts.

categories.name: Change Preventers
categories.description: Smells that cause the slightest change to one part of the system to require cascading edits in multiple other places.

subcategories.name: Modification Friction
subcategories.description: Violation of the single responsibility principle and high coupling of modification logic.

subcategories.name: Parallel Structures
subcategories.description: Coupled hierarchies that require synchronous duplication of class structure.

categories.name: Dispensables
categories.description: Meaningless, empty, dead, or duplicate elements whose removal cleans up and simplifies the codebase.

subcategories.name: Code Redundancy
subcategories.description: Repetition of algorithms and data structures across different parts of the program.

subcategories.name: Dead & Lazy Entities
subcategories.description: Code that is no longer used, or classes that do not justify their existence.

subcategories.name: Overengineering
subcategories.description: Speculative abstractions and deodorant comments masking poor design.

categories.name: Couplers
categories.description: Smells that contribute to excessive coupling between classes or violate encapsulation for the sake of intermediary calls.

subcategories.name: Inappropriate Coupling
subcategories.description: Excessive interest of a class in the internals of other classes or violation of encapsulation.

subcategories.name: Delegation Distortion
subcategories.description: Message chains through third-party objects or middleman classes that merely forward calls.

categories.name: Functional & Algorithmic Smells
categories.description: Issues with algorithmic logic, uncontrolled state mutations, hidden side effects, and tangled control flow.

subcategories.name: Side Effects & Mutations
subcategories.description: Mutation of input parameters, hidden dependencies on external state, and impure functions.

subcategories.name: Control Flow Complexity
subcategories.description: Deep nesting, flag arguments, temporal coupling, and magic constants.

categories.name: Error & Exception Handling
categories.description: Antipatterns of catching, raising, and handling exceptions that mask failures and disrupt debugging.

subcategories.name: Exception Masking & Swallowing
subcategories.description: Swallowing exceptions, loss of trace context, and catching the base Exception type.

subcategories.name: Flow & Contract Abuse
subcategories.description: Using exceptions for control flow branching and returning null instead of explicit failure types.

categories.name: Concurrency & Asynchrony
categories.description: Synchronization errors, race conditions, deadlocks, and incorrect usage of asynchronous primitives.

subcategories.name: Race & Locking Hazards
subcategories.description: Unprotected shared state, busy waiting, and locking errors.

subcategories.name: Async Anti-Patterns
subcategories.description: Blocking calls to asynchronous operations (Sync over Async) and uncontrolled launching of tasks.

categories.name: Architecture & System Design
categories.description: Global design smells affecting inter-module boundaries, circular dependencies, and layer integrity.

subcategories.name: Architectural Coupling
subcategories.description: Cycles in module dependencies, leaky abstractions, and rigid configuration.

subcategories.name: Layer & Interface Degradation
subcategories.description: Violation of layer purity, bloated interfaces, and spaghetti structures.

categories.name: Test Smells
categories.description: Design and implementation defects of unit and integration tests leading to their instability and reading difficulties.

subcategories.name: Test Structure & Semantics
subcategories.description: Opaque fixtures, greedy tests, and multiple assertions without context.

subcategories.name: Test Reliability & Decay
subcategories.description: Flaky tests due to timeouts, conditional logic, and forgotten disabled checks.

categories.name: Database & Persistence
categories.description: Suboptimal database interaction patterns, ORM pitfalls, and query generation vulnerabilities.

subcategories.name: ORM & Query Efficiency
subcategories.description: The N+1 query problem, excessive data loading into memory, and absence of required indexes.

subcategories.name: Schema Design & Integrity
subcategories.description: Monster tables and unsafe SQL query concatenation.

categories.name: Security & Resource Management
categories.description: Code patterns leading to security vulnerabilities, confidential data leaks, and system descriptor leaks.

subcategories.name: Security Vulnerabilities
subcategories.description: Hardcoding secrets, disabling SSL/TLS verification, and logging personal data (PII).

subcategories.name: Resource Hygiene
subcategories.description: Leaks of open file descriptors, sockets, and pool connections.

categories.name: Frontend & UI Components
categories.description: Specific smells of modern UI libraries and frameworks (React, Vue, Angular): reactivity, state, and effects.

subcategories.name: Component State & Dataflow
subcategories.description: Prop drilling across dozens of levels, duplication of derived state, and god components.

subcategories.name: Lifecycle & DOM Reactivity
subcategories.description: Direct DOM intervention and forgotten unsubscriptions in lifecycle hooks.

smells.name: Long Method
smells.summary: A method containing too many lines of code, mixing different levels of abstraction, and solving several tasks simultaneously.
smells.definition: A code smell where the body of a function or method exceeds a reasonable size (usually over 20-30 lines of code), combining business logic, validation, data formatting, and low-level operations, which complicates its understanding, maintenance, and isolated testing.
symptoms: The method does not fit on one editor screen and requires constant scrolling
Inside the method, there are blocks of code with explanatory comments before each step ('// Step 1: Validation', '// Step 2: Discount calculation')
The method contains many local variables with a wide scope
High cyclomatic complexity (many nested loops and if/else conditions)
It is difficult to give the method a simple and precise name without the conjunction 'and'
root_causes: Incremental development: each developer added 2-3 lines for a new feature
Violation of the Single Responsibility Principle (SRP)
Fear of function call overhead (an obsolete myth)
Reluctance to think through abstractions and create new private methods
impact: A sharp increase in cognitive load on developers when reading code
Increased risk of introducing regression bugs during any changes
Inability to reuse individual fragments of logic
Extremely hindered unit testing (requires preparing a huge number of mocks)

refactoring_techniques.name: Extract Method (Extraction of Method)
refactoring_techniques.description: Extracting a logically isolated group of lines into a separate method with an intention-revealing name.

refactoring_techniques.name: Replace Temp with Query (Replacing Temporary Variable with Method Call)
refactoring_techniques.description: Eliminating intermediate local variables by converting calculations into functions.

refactoring_techniques.name: Decompose Conditional (Decomposition of Conditional Statements)
refactoring_techniques.description: Extracting complex predicates and conditional branch bodies into separate understandable methods.

refactoring_techniques.name: Preserve Whole Object (Preserving the Whole Object)
refactoring_techniques.description: Passing the original object as a whole instead of unpacking a dozen of its fields into arguments.

bad_example.explanation: The `processOrder` method performs 5 disparate responsibilities: order validation, mathematical calculation and application of discounts, financial transaction, direct manipulation of inventory balances in the database, and generation of email notifications. Changing any of these steps forces modifying one huge method.

good_example.explanation: The method is reduced to 5 declarative top-level coordination lines. Each phase is encapsulated in a specialized service covered by isolated tests. The SRP (Single Responsibility Principle) is adhered to.

smells.name: Large Class / God Class
smells.summary: A class that has absorbed too many responsibilities, fields, and methods, becoming the central hub of all system logic.
smells.definition: An anti-pattern and design smell where a single class assumes control over the vast majority of domain processes, accumulating hundreds of methods and dozens of fields. Meanwhile, the remaining classes of the system degenerate into passive data structures.
symptoms: The class file contains hundreds or thousands of lines of code
The class has dozens of private and public fields
Different groups of methods use completely disjoint subsets of class fields (low cohesion — Low Cohesion)
Dependencies flow into the class from virtually all application subsystems
Constant merge conflicts in the version control system due to edits by different developers
root_causes: Feature creep inertia: it is easier to add a method to an existing 'working' class than to create a new one
Lack of timely domain decomposition into bounded contexts (Bounded Contexts)
Misunderstanding of the single responsibility principle
impact: Extremely high system coupling and impossibility of isolated testing
Difficulty of understanding: no single developer can keep the class architecture in their head
Any local change can unpredictably break an unrelated scenario

refactoring_techniques.name: Extract Class (Extracting a Class)
refactoring_techniques.description: Grouping related fields and methods into a separate class with a clearly delineated responsibility.

refactoring_techniques.name: Extract Subclass (Extracting a Subclass)
refactoring_techniques.description: Extracting specific behaviors for individual subtypes of an entity into subclasses.

refactoring_techniques.name: Extract Interface (Extracting an Interface)
refactoring_techniques.description: Splitting the facade of a large class into multiple narrowly focused interfaces (ISP).

bad_example.explanation: The `UserManager` class combines authentication management, payment gateway, billing, report generation, analytics, and user administration. It is a clear case of a classic 'God Object'.

good_example.explanation: The monolithic class is decomposed into four specialized services with high cohesion (High Cohesion). Each class is responsible for exactly one area and is easily tested.

smells.name: Primitive Obsession
smells.summary: Using basic primitive data types (numbers, strings, arrays) instead of creating dedicated domain objects (Value Objects).
smells.definition: A code smell in which domain concepts (money, phone numbers, date ranges, postal addresses, units of measure) are modeled using primitives (string, number, float). As a result, the validation and formatting logic for this data is smeared with duplication across the entire codebase.
symptoms: Widespread use of string constants to identify types, statuses, or currencies
Multiple duplication of regular expressions for email or phone number validation across different methods
Accidental passing of parameters of the same type in the wrong order (for example, `transfer(sourceAccountId: string, destAccountId: string, amount: number)`)
Calculations with money or physical quantities are conducted without taking currency or units of measurement into account
root_causes: The habit of viewing classes only as 'heavy' entities, reluctance to create micro-types
Outdated limitations of older versions of programming languages
Blind trust in types coming from external JSON APIs or databases
impact: Vulnerabilities and hidden bugs: occurrences of negative amounts, invalid emails, empty identifiers
Duplication of validation and formatting logic across dozens of classes
Loss of expressiveness of the domain model (Type Safety)

detection_metrics.primitive_fields_ratio: > 80% of entity fields have string/number/boolean types
detection_metrics.string_validation_duplicates: Repetition of regular expressions or checks in >= 3 places

refactoring_techniques.name: Replace Data Value with Object (Replacing Data Value with Object)
refactoring_techniques.description: Creating a Value Object (an immutable value object) that encapsulates validation and rules.

refactoring_techniques.name: Replace Type Code with Class / Subclasses / Enum
refactoring_techniques.description: Transforming string or integer type codes into enumerations or a class hierarchy.

refactoring_techniques.name: Introduce Parameter Object (Introducing a Parameter Object)
refactoring_techniques.description: Combining related primitives (e.g., start_date, end_date) into a single DateRange structure.

bad_example.explanation: Account number, money, and currency are passed as primitives. It is easy to mix up `senderAccount` and `recipientAccount`, pass a negative commission, or add an amount in USD to an amount in EUR without conversion.

good_example.explanation: Domain value objects `IbanAccount` and `Money` have been created. The compiler protects against accidental argument substitution, and validation and addition rules are encapsulated inside the classes.

smells.name: Long Parameter List
smells.summary: A method or constructor accepts too many arguments (more than 3-4), making it difficult to call and prone to errors.
smells.definition: A code smell that occurs when overloading a method signature with an excessive number of formal parameters. When calling such a method, it is extremely difficult to remember the correct order of arguments without IDE hints, and adding a new parameter breaks compatibility across all call sites.
symptoms: Function signature contains 5 or more parameters
Several consecutive arguments of the same type appear in the parameter list (for example, three booleans or four strings)
Developers pass `null` or default values in half of the function calls
To call the function, arguments have to be wrapped across multiple lines
root_causes: An attempt to make the method an all-in-one 'combine harvester' for all scenarios
Reluctance to create intermediate data structures / DTOs
Passing data for dependent computations instead of passing a data provider
impact: High probability of confusing the order of parameters of the same type during invocation
Interface fragility: changing a signature requires refactoring dozens of call sites
Difficulty reading and maintaining unit tests

detection_metrics.consecutive_same_type_params: >= 3 parameters of the same type in a row

refactoring_techniques.name: Introduce Parameter Object
refactoring_techniques.description: Combining a group of arguments into a separate class or interface (Config/Options/DTO).

refactoring_techniques.name: Preserve Whole Object
refactoring_techniques.description: Passing the original domain model object instead of extracting and passing its individual fields.

refactoring_techniques.name: Replace Parameter with Method Call
refactoring_techniques.description: Obtaining the parameter value inside the called method if it has access to the data source.

refactoring_techniques.name: Builder Pattern
refactoring_techniques.description: Applying the Builder pattern for fluent call configuration.

bad_example.explanation: 11 parameters in the signature. Mixing up `departmentId` and `reportsToManagerId` or two adjacent boolean flags `isRemote` and `hasHealthInsurance` is possible without a single compiler error.

good_example.explanation: Arguments are divided into logical groups within typed structures `PersonalDetails` and `EmploymentTerms`. Call-site code becomes self-documenting and safe.

smells.name: Data Clumps
smells.summary: Groups of variables or parameters that constantly appear together across different classes and method signatures.
smells.definition: A code smell where the same 3-4 variables travel together from class to class, are passed as a bundle of parameters into various methods, or are declared synchronously across multiple data structures, yet have still not been encapsulated into a separate class.
symptoms: Triplets of fields like `city`, `street`, `zipCode` repeat across `Order`, `Customer`, `Invoice`
Pairs of `startDate`, `endDate` wander across a dozen function signatures of reports and filters
When deleting one of these fields, it must be synchronously removed from multiple classes and methods
root_causes: Procedural mindset of developers
Reluctance to create lightweight conceptual domain entities
impact: Duplication of field descriptions and their types across different parts of the system
Lack of a single place to encapsulate business rules associated with this group of fields (for example, date range validation)

detection_metrics.clump_frequency: Match of a group of >= 3 fields across >= 2 different classes or signatures

refactoring_techniques.name: Extract Class
refactoring_techniques.description: Combining a repeating group of fields into an independent class.

refactoring_techniques.name: Introduce Parameter Object
refactoring_techniques.description: Replacing a repeating group of method parameters with a single object.

refactoring_techniques.name: Preserve Whole Object
refactoring_techniques.description: Passing the created object as a whole instead of unpacking it into separate parameters.

bad_example.explanation: The triplet of fields (city, street, zipCode) is duplicated both in the fields of the `ShippingOrder` and `Warehouse` classes and in the route calculation method signature.

good_example.explanation: An `Address` class has been extracted. Related data and its formatting logic are encapsulated in a single place, and method signatures have become concise.

smells.name: Combinatorial Explosion
smells.summary: An avalanche-like growth in the number of methods to support all possible combinations of arguments, formats, or query parameters.
smells.definition: A code smell where, instead of using flexible compositional patterns (such as Strategy, Builder, or Specification), a separate method is added to a class for each combination of conditions or input/output formats (for example, `findByName`, `findByNameAndAge`, `findByNameAndAgeAndCity`).
symptoms: A class contains dozens of similar variations of the same method with minor differences in the parameter set
Adding a single new filtering criterion requires writing a dozen new methods
Duplication of 90% of the implementation code between these methods
root_causes: Ignoring design patterns for dynamic filtering (Specification, Criteria, Query Object)
Attempting to solve the problem with method overloading without changing the architectural approach
impact: Bloating the class to hundreds of lines of boilerplate code
High maintenance cost and inability to support complex composite queries

detection_metrics.similar_method_names_count: >= 5 methods with the same prefix and variations of suffixes

refactoring_techniques.name: Query Object / Specification Pattern
refactoring_techniques.description: Creating a query object with free composition of predicates.

refactoring_techniques.name: Builder Pattern
refactoring_techniques.description: Building query parameters via a chain of builder method calls.

bad_example.explanation: A new method is written in the repository for each field combination. With 5 fields, the number of combinations can exceed dozens of methods.

good_example.explanation: A single specification object `UserQuerySpecification` is used. One universal `Find` method covers any combination of conditions without bloating the codebase.

smells.name: Long Chain of Calls / Train Wreck
smells.name_en: Long Chain of Calls / Train Wreck
smells.summary: A chain of consecutive method calls navigating through internal objects, tightly coupling the code to the object graph.
smells.definition: A code smell that occurs when client code calls a method on one object, then calls the next method on the returned object, and so on (for example, `a.getB().getC().getD().doSomething()`). This is a flagrant violation of the Law of Demeter, creating excessive coupling to the internal topology of the system.
symptoms: Multiple dots or access operators in a row in a single line (`order.getCustomer().getAddress().getCountry().getCode()`)
High probability of crashing with `NullPointerException` / `TypeError: cannot read property of null` at any link in the chain
Any change to an intermediate class breaks the calling code in dozens of places
root_causes: Disregarding the Law of Demeter ('talk only to your immediate friends')
Blurred responsibility and lack of delegating methods in intermediate classes
Treating objects as transparent data structures
impact: Extremely fragile code: changing the structure of internal relationships requires refactoring all clients
Difficulty of unit testing: having to mock the entire chain of intermediate objects

detection_metrics.navigation_depth: > 2 consecutive navigation calls in a row (excluding Fluent APIs and builders)
detection_metrics.law_of_demeter_violations: Calling methods on objects that are not parameters, fields, or locally created objects

refactoring_techniques.name: Hide Delegate (Hiding Delegation)
refactoring_techniques.description: Adding a delegate method to the nearest object to hide the chain.

refactoring_techniques.name: Extract Method & Move Method
refactoring_techniques.description: Moving logic closer to the target object that owns the processed data.

bad_example.explanation: The `InvoiceService` class is aware of the structure of `Order`, `Customer`, `Profile`, and `BillingDetails`. If a field moves from `Profile` to `Customer`, `InvoiceService` breaks.

good_example.explanation: The chain is hidden thanks to delegation. The client only communicates with `Order`, and the internal structure is hidden in accordance with the Law of Demeter.

smells.name: Switch Statements / Complex Conditionals
smells.summary: Using branching switch statements or if-else chains to select behavior based on an object's type instead of polymorphism.
smells.definition: A code smell that occurs when the choice of logic to execute depends on a type code (Type Code) or enumeration (Enum) and is implemented via switch/case statements scattered across multiple methods or classes in the system. When a new type is added, one has to manually find and update all of these switch statements.
symptoms: The same `switch(type)` is repeated across different methods (cost calculation, validation, UI display, JSON export)
Long chains of `if (type == A) ... else if (type == B) ...`
Adding a new type requires modifying multiple files and easily leads to missing one of the branches
High cyclomatic complexity of methods
root_causes: Procedural programming habits in object-oriented code
Fear of creating classes and polymorphism hierarchies
Storing types as string constants or integers
impact: Violation of the Open/Closed Principle
High risk of regression defects due to forgotten switch branches
Difficulty of extending the system with third-party plugins or modules

detection_metrics.repeated_switch_on_same_type: Repeating selection based on the same type in >= 2 places

refactoring_techniques.name: Replace Conditional with Polymorphism (Replacing Conditional with Polymorphism)
refactoring_techniques.description: Creating subclasses or interface implementations with a specialized method.

refactoring_techniques.name: Replace Type Code with Subclasses
refactoring_techniques.description: Transforming an encoded type into polymorphic descendants of a base class.

refactoring_techniques.name: Strategy Pattern / State Pattern
refactoring_techniques.description: Extracting the variable algorithm into separate strategy objects.

bad_example.explanation: The same switch is duplicated in calculating bonuses and vacation days. Adding a `DESIGNER` role will force finding and editing all methods of the `Payroll` class.

good_example.explanation: Polymorphism is applied (Strategy pattern). Adding the `DesignerRole` role does not require editing existing code (OCP), and all role properties are consolidated in a single class.

smells.name: Refused Bequest
smells.summary: A subclass uses only a small portion of inherited methods or overrides parent methods by throwing an UnsupportedOperationException.
smells.definition: An object-oriented design smell where a child class inherits behavior or data from a parent class, but does not actually need them or they contradict its semantics. This is a direct violation of the Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP).
symptoms: Overridden parent methods contain empty bodies or throw `UnsupportedOperationException` / `NotImplementedError`
Clients are forced to check the actual type of an object before calling an inherited method
Refusal to use most fields and properties of the base class
root_causes: Using inheritance solely for the sake of reusing a couple of lines of code rather than creating an 'is-a' relationship
Flawed or overly generalized taxonomy of base classes
impact: Violation of polymorphism: substituting a subclass breaks client code at runtime
Unexpected program crashes at runtime
Distortion of the system's conceptual model

detection_metrics.empty_overrides_count: >= 1 parent methods are overridden with an empty body or throw a 'not supported' exception
detection_metrics.unused_inherited_methods: > 40% of base class methods make no sense for the descendant

refactoring_techniques.name: Replace Inheritance with Delegation
refactoring_techniques.description: Injecting the former parent class as a field and delegating only the required calls.

refactoring_techniques.name: Extract Superclass
refactoring_techniques.description: Creating a common ancestor with minimal shared behavior for both classes.

bad_example.explanation: The `Penguin` class inherits from `Bird`, but refuses the `fly()` method. Client code `birds.forEach(b => b.fly())` will crash with an error on a penguin.

good_example.explanation: The base class `Bird` contains only behavior common to all birds. The ability to fly is extracted into a specialized `FlyingAnimal` interface, adhering to the LSP principle.

smells.name: Alternative Classes with Different Interfaces
smells.summary: Two or more classes solve an identical task, but have different method names and incompatible signatures.
smells.definition: A code smell that occurs when several classes perform functionally identical operations (for example, sending messages, exporting files, or calculating routes), but their methods are named differently (for example, `sendNotification` vs `pushMessage`) and do not implement a unified interface.
symptoms: The project has classes with similar purposes, but clients cannot use them interchangeably
Client code has to write adapters or conditions like `if (provider is ServiceA) ... else ...`
Duplication of adaptation logic when invoking different classes
root_causes: Independent development of modules by different programmers without prior coordination of interfaces
Integration of third-party libraries without an abstraction layer
impact: Inability to polymorphically substitute components
Code duplication and proliferation of conditionals in client code

detection_metrics.semantic_overlap: Classes have > 70% semantically matching functions in the absence of a common interface

refactoring_techniques.name: Rename Method
refactoring_techniques.description: Bringing method names and signatures to a single standard.

refactoring_techniques.name: Extract Interface
refactoring_techniques.description: Creating a common interface implemented by both classes.

refactoring_techniques.name: Adapter Pattern
refactoring_techniques.description: Wrapping an incompatible class in an adapter if the source code cannot be changed.

bad_example.explanation: Two SMS providers have different method names and return types. The client is forced to write type-checking conditions instead of making a polymorphic call.

good_example.explanation: A unified `SmsGateway` interface is extracted and the Adapter pattern is applied. The client interacts with the contract and does not depend on implementation details.

smells.name: Temporary Field
smells.summary: A class field that holds a value only during the execution of specific calculations or in special circumstances, and equals null the rest of the time.
smells.definition: A code smell where a variable needed only by one specific algorithm or method is exposed to the class state. For the rest of the object's lifetime, this field remains empty (`null`/`undefined`), misleading developers regarding the object's actual invariant.
symptoms: The field is initialized only inside one specific method and is reset to null after its completion
Constant `if (this.temporaryResult != null)` checks across different parts of the class
The object cannot be safely used in a multithreaded environment because the temporary field causes a data race
root_causes: Reluctance to pass intermediate values via parameter calls of private methods
An attempt to avoid creating a result object for a complex calculation
impact: Violation of thread safety (Race Condition during concurrent calls)
Difficulty in understanding the class lifecycle and invariants
`NullPointerException` errors when calling methods in an unexpected order

detection_metrics.field_usage_scope: The field is used in only 1 or 2 related methods out of all methods in the class
detection_metrics.nullable_lifecycle: The field is null in most lifecycle states

refactoring_techniques.name: Extract Class (Method Object)
refactoring_techniques.description: Moving the algorithm and its temporary variables into a separate execution object (Command/Query).

refactoring_techniques.name: Introduce Null Object / Result Object
refactoring_techniques.description: Returning a separate object with results instead of mutating fields of the current instance.

bad_example.explanation: The `_cachedTaxRate` and `_intermediateDeductions` fields are temporary. If the `Calculate` method is called simultaneously from two threads, they will overwrite each other's values.

good_example.explanation: Temporary fields have been eliminated. Values are stored in method local variables (on the thread stack), which makes the class completely thread-safe and gives it a clear invariant.

smells.name: Anemic Domain Model
smells.summary: Entity classes contain only fields, getters, and setters, while all business logic is moved into giant service classes.
smells.definition: An object-oriented design anti-pattern described by Martin Fowler. Domain entities turn into passive 'data bags' without any behavior or validation, while logic and invariant verification are scattered across dozens of external services.
symptoms: Entity classes consist only of public getters and setters without business methods
Service classes contain all logic for validation, modification, and state transitions
Any external code can put an entity into an inconsistent or invalid state via a public setter
root_causes: Misunderstanding of layered architecture (perceiving entities as simple reflections of database tables)
Influence of procedural programming style
impact: Complete loss of encapsulation: entity invariants are not guaranteed
Duplication of business rules across different services
Degeneration of the object-oriented paradigm back into a procedural style

detection_metrics.getters_setters_ratio: 100% of class methods are simple getters/setters
detection_metrics.entity_business_methods: 0 business methods in the domain entity class

refactoring_techniques.name: Move Method
refactoring_techniques.description: Moving business logic and validations from services directly into the domain entity.

refactoring_techniques.name: Encapsulate Field
refactoring_techniques.description: Closing public setters and allowing modification only through meaningful methods (for example, `cancel()`, `applyDiscount()`).

bad_example.explanation: The `BankAccount` entity does not protect its invariants. Any service can execute `account.balance = -999999` directly without checks.

good_example.explanation: Rich Domain Model. The entity completely encapsulates its state and business rules, making it impossible to put the object into an invalid state.

smells.name: Type Introspection and Downcasting
smells.summary: Using type check operators (instanceof, is, as) to determine an object's concrete class followed by forced type casting.
smells.definition: A code smell in which the polymorphic contract is ignored, and calling code explicitly checks whether an object belongs to a concrete derived class using operators such as `instanceof` / `is` / `dynamic_cast`. This is a sign of a poorly designed common interface.
symptoms: Constructs like `if (shape instanceof Circle) { ((Circle) shape).getRadius(); }`
Constantly casting a base type to specific derived classes
Runtime occurrences of `ClassCastException`
root_causes: Lack of the required polymorphic operation in the base interface
An attempt to combine fundamentally different entities into a single hierarchy
impact: Tight coupling to concrete implementations instead of abstractions
Violation of the Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP) and the Open-Closed Principle (OCP)

detection_metrics.instanceof_checks_count: >= 2 instanceof checks in a single conditional block

refactoring_techniques.name: Replace Conditional with Polymorphism
refactoring_techniques.description: Adding the required abstract method to the base interface.

refactoring_techniques.name: Visitor Pattern
refactoring_techniques.description: Applying the Visitor pattern if the class structure cannot be changed.

bad_example.explanation: The `renderShape` method descends into knowing the details of all possible shapes via `instanceof` and forced casting.

good_example.explanation: Each shape knows how to draw itself. The `renderShape` method contains no type checks and is easily extended with new shapes.

smells.name: Freeloader / Marker Interface Abuse
smells.summary: Using empty marker interfaces instead of modern annotations/attributes, or creating interfaces for the sake of a single trivial implementation.
smells.definition: A code smell consisting of abusing interfaces without methods to mark object behavior (marker interfaces), or creating an interface for every class in a project without any real need for alternative implementations (blindly following the 'one class, one interface' rule).
symptoms: Empty interfaces without a single method (`interface Cacheable {}`)
Checking marker membership via `instanceof` in business logic
`IFoo` interfaces that have exactly one implementation `Foo` and will never be replaced or mocked
root_causes: Outdated habits from early language versions when annotations/attributes did not yet exist
The dogmatic rule 'every class must have an interface' without understanding the purposes
impact: Cluttering the codebase with empty abstractions
Doubling the number of files requiring synchronous editing

detection_metrics.one_to_one_implementations: The interface is implemented by exactly one class and is not used for mocks

refactoring_techniques.name: Replace Marker Interface with Annotation / Attribute
refactoring_techniques.description: Replacing an empty interface with metadata (decorator/annotation).

refactoring_techniques.name: Inline Interface
refactoring_techniques.description: Eliminating the single-implementation interface and directly using the class if polymorphism is not required.

bad_example.explanation: Using an empty interface as a marker pollutes the type hierarchy and forces the use of the `is` type check operator.

good_example.explanation: The interface is replaced with a declarative attribute/annotation that does not pollute the OOP type system.

smells.name: Divergent Change
smells.summary: A single class has to be modified for completely different reasons and when unrelated business requirements change.
smells.definition: A code smell that violates the Single Responsibility Principle (SRP). It occurs when a single class combines multiple disparate areas of responsibility. When the database schema changes, class X has to be edited; when page rendering rules change, the same class X; when the tax formula changes, class X again.
symptoms: When viewing git commit history, it is evident that the exact same file is edited when performing absolutely any task
Developers from different teams regularly encounter merge conflicts when merging changes into this class
It is difficult to formulate the class's purpose in a single phrase without using the word 'also'
root_causes: Concentrating related operations in one place 'for convenience'
Insufficient architectural modularity and non-compliance with SRP
impact: High regression risk: modifying the export format can break tax calculation
Constant merge conflicts in the version control system
Code review difficulty due to giant diffs

detection_metrics.git_churn_rate: High file change frequency in commit history (> 30% of commits affect this file)
detection_metrics.different_actors_count: Changes are initiated by unrelated business stakeholders

refactoring_techniques.name: Extract Class
refactoring_techniques.description: Splitting behavior into separate classes depending on the reasons for changes.

refactoring_techniques.name: Separate Domain and Presentation
refactoring_techniques.description: Isolating business rules from the user interface and database persistence.

bad_example.explanation: The `AccountManager` class changes for 3 different reasons: financial rule edits, UI redesign, and database migrations. This is a classic Divergent Change.

good_example.explanation: Responsibilities are split into three independent classes, each with a single reason to change.

smells.name: Shotgun Surgery
smells.summary: Making a single small change to logic requires edits across dozens of different files and classes throughout the project.
smells.definition: The code smell that is the inverse of Divergent Change. When a single business change occurs (for example, adding a new order status or a new field to an entity), the developer has to 'fire a shotgun' — open and manually edit 10-20 different files, risking forgetting one of them.
symptoms: A single commit or pull request involves microscopic edits across 15+ files
Identical switch/if branches based on the same condition are smeared across services, controllers, repositories, and tests
Frequent omissions of edits in one of the files, leading to bugs in production
root_causes: Excessive scattering of a single responsibility across multiple small classes
Lack of centralized encapsulation of a domain concept
impact: High effort required even for the simplest modifications
Critical probability of missing one of the files during manual refactoring

detection_metrics.files_modified_per_feature: Regular commits with > 10 modified files for the sake of a single trivial task

refactoring_techniques.name: Move Method / Move Field
refactoring_techniques.description: Gathering all disparate parts of behavior into a single common target class.

refactoring_techniques.name: Inline Class
refactoring_techniques.description: Combining excessively fragmented classes into a single full-fledged entity.

bad_example.explanation: The concept of order status and all reactions associated with it are smeared across 6 different unrelated files. If the developer forgets to update `AccountingReport`, the report will diverge from the cash register.

good_example.explanation: Behavior is localized in a state object/handler. Adding a new status occurs by adding a single handler class without shotgun surgery across other files.

smells.name: Parallel Inheritance Hierarchies
smells.summary: Creating a subclass in one hierarchy inevitably requires synchronously creating a subclass in another hierarchy.
smells.definition: A code smell where every time you create a subclass for one class (for example, `SqlDataSource` for `DataSource`), you are required to create a corresponding subclass in a completely different hierarchy (for example, `SqlQueryBuilder` for `QueryBuilder`).
symptoms: Prefixes or suffixes of classes from the two hierarchies mirror each other (`PdfReport` -> `PdfReportRenderer`, `ExcelReport` -> `ExcelReportRenderer`)
It is impossible to add a single feature without simultaneously extending both parallel class chains
root_causes: Artificial splitting of responsibilities between two parallel inheritance trees
Incorrect application of the Abstract Factory pattern without necessity
impact: Doubling the number of created classes
Synchronous coupling of two inheritance trees

detection_metrics.mirror_hierarchy_depth: Two or more inheritance trees with identical node names and identical depth

refactoring_techniques.name: Move Method / Move Field
refactoring_techniques.description: Collapsing one of the hierarchies into the other via delegation.

refactoring_techniques.name: Bridge Pattern
refactoring_techniques.description: Weakening the coupling between abstraction and implementation.

bad_example.explanation: When adding a new instrument `Flute`, the developer is required to add both `Flute` and `FluteController`. Two hierarchies evolve in parallel.

good_example.explanation: Hierarchies are eliminated through composition and behavior delegation. New entities are created via instantiation without multiplying pairs of classes.

smells.name: Duplicate Code
smells.summary: Identical or nearly identical code fragments occur in two or more places in the application.
smells.definition: One of the most dangerous and frequent code smells. Occurs when a developer copies a block of code instead of extracting a shared function, method, or component. As a result, when fixing a bug in the original, the copy remains unfixed, giving rise to hidden regression bugs.
symptoms: Identical lines of code or conditional structures across different files
Code differs only by the names of a couple of local variables
A bug once fixed in one service reproduces again in another place
root_causes: Haste and deadline pressure ('copied, tested, works')
Reluctance or fear of modifying someone else's code to extract a shared abstraction
Insufficient knowledge of the standard library and utilities that already exist in the project
impact: Double, triple waste of time maintaining the same algorithm
High risk of logic desynchronization: a bug is resolved in one place but remains in copies

detection_metrics.token_similarity: > 85% token match in blocks of 6 or more lines
detection_metrics.cpd_findings: Detection of duplicates by tools like SonarQube / PMD-CPD

refactoring_techniques.name: Extract Method
refactoring_techniques.description: Extracting the duplicate fragment into a single shared method.

refactoring_techniques.name: Pull Up Method
refactoring_techniques.description: Moving the shared method to a superclass if duplication arose in subclasses.

refactoring_techniques.name: Form Template Method
refactoring_techniques.description: Generalizing similar algorithms with variations in individual steps.

bad_example.explanation: The CSV escaping algorithm is copied entirely. If escaping rules change, one of the methods will inevitably be forgotten to be updated.

good_example.explanation: The string formatting logic and loop are extracted into a generalized function (DRY — Don't Repeat Yourself).

smells.name: Dead Code
smells.summary: Variables, parameters, methods, or entire classes that are never called or used in the application.
smells.definition: A code smell representing remnants of old functionality, unreachable conditional branches, unused imports, commented-out pieces of code, or private methods whose calls have been deleted. They clutter the project and waste engineers' attention.
symptoms: Compiler or linter warnings about unused identifiers
Blocks of commented-out code marked 'just in case'
Conditions that mathematically can never be true (`if (false)` or unreachable code after return)
root_causes: Removing functionality without cleaning up helper methods
Fear of deleting code ('what if it comes in handy later')
Not using static analyzers in the CI/CD pipeline
impact: Distracting developers' attention to reading and mentally maintaining useless code
Increase in bundle size and compilation/build time

detection_metrics.zero_references: Public/private methods with 0 real references in the entire repository

refactoring_techniques.name: Delete Code
refactoring_techniques.description: Deleting dead code without regret: the version control system (git) will always preserve history.

refactoring_techniques.name: Inline Method
refactoring_techniques.description: Inlining a method if it is called in only one dead scenario.

bad_example.explanation: The commented-out call and orphaned private method `calculateOldShipping` hang as dead weight, confusing new developers.

good_example.explanation: All unused code and comments have been deleted. If the old algorithm is ever needed, it can be easily retrieved from git history.

smells.name: Lazy Class / Freeloader
smells.summary: A class that does too little to justify its separate existence and maintenance overhead.
smells.definition: A code smell in which a class is virtually devoid of logic — containing 1-2 trivial methods, acting merely as a pointless layer, or the class was once full-fledged, but after refactoring only a remnant remains of it.
symptoms: The class consists of a single microscopic method called in one place
The class computes nothing and merely passes data along without changes
root_causes: Excessive atomization of architecture ('fanatical micro-decomposition')
Shrinking of the class during prolonged refactorings
impact: Increased mental complexity of the system: having to remember dozens of micro-classes
Overhead of navigating the project's file system

detection_metrics.lines_of_code_loc: < 15 lines of useful code in the class

refactoring_techniques.name: Inline Class (Inlining a Class)
refactoring_techniques.description: Merging the lazy class with the calling or target class.

refactoring_techniques.name: Collapse Hierarchy (Collapsing a Hierarchy)
refactoring_techniques.description: Merging a subclass with its parent if the subclass hardly differs from it.

bad_example.explanation: Creating a separate class for the sake of a standard library call `ToUpperInvariant()` unreasonably complicates the architecture.

good_example.explanation: The redundant class is eliminated, and the method is inlined at the call site.

smells.name: Data Class
smells.summary: The class contains only data fields and trivial access methods (getters/setters), having no behavior whatsoever.
smells.definition: A code smell where a class is a dumb data container. Manipulations of this class's fields are performed by other objects from the outside. This provokes the emergence of Feature Envy in other classes.
symptoms: There is not a single algorithmic or business method in the class
All processing of the class's data is concentrated in other services
root_causes: Relational modeling habits without combining data with operations on it
Procedural thinking
impact: Smearing business rules across external services
Difficulty of maintaining state invariants

detection_metrics.methods_to_fields_ratio: Methods are limited only to get/set for each field

refactoring_techniques.name: Move Method (Moving a Method)
refactoring_techniques.description: Moving data processing logic from external classes inside the data class.

refactoring_techniques.name: Encapsulate Field
refactoring_techniques.description: Hiding fields and providing meaningful operations.

bad_example.explanation: The `Rectangle` class is passive. Area calculation is moved to an external `GeometryService` service, which severs data and behavior.

good_example.explanation: Area calculation logic and validation are encapsulated within the `Rectangle` class itself.

smells.name: Speculative Generality
smells.summary: Creating complex abstractions, hooks, parameters, and class hierarchies in reserve for non-existent future requirements.
smells.definition: A design smell where the developer tries to predict future business needs and overcomplicates the code in advance with generic interfaces, factories of factories, and abstract layers that in reality will never be needed (a violation of the YAGNI principle — You Aren't Gonna Need It).
symptoms: Interfaces and abstract classes having exactly one descendant in the project
Methods accept unused parameters with comments 'reserved for future'
Unjustifiably complex configuration factories for trivial actions
root_causes: Astronaut syndrome (Architecture Astronauts)
The desire to write a 'perfect extensible system' instead of solving the current task
impact: High cost of understanding and maintaining the system
Future real requirements almost always do not match speculative fantasies, and the abstractions have to be reworked

detection_metrics.unused_abstractions_count: Abstract classes or generics with 1 trivial type parameter

refactoring_techniques.name: Collapse Hierarchy (Collapsing a Hierarchy)
refactoring_techniques.description: Elimination of unnecessary superclasses and lone interfaces.

refactoring_techniques.name: Remove Parameter (Removing a Parameter)
refactoring_techniques.description: Removal of unused reserved parameters.

bad_example.explanation: Architectural overhead: 5 generic parameters for the sake of an elementary user repository.

good_example.explanation: A simple, straightforward repository class. If complex scenarios arise in the future, they will be added as they occur (YAGNI).

smells.name: Comments as Deodorant
smells.summary: Using comments to explain convoluted, poor-quality, or poorly named code instead of refactoring it.
smells.definition: A code smell where a comment serves as a 'deodorant' for bad-smelling code. The developer writes a convoluted algorithm or gives vague variable names (`x1`, `tmp`), and then adds a paragraph of comments trying to explain what this code does.
symptoms: Comments recount what the code on the adjacent line does (`// increment i by 1`)
A complex block of 40 lines is preceded by the comment `// Magic: checking session validity`
Comments are outdated and contradict the actual behavior of the code
root_causes: Laziness to refactor and give descriptive names to methods and variables
Following outdated guidelines ('every line must be commented')
impact: Over time, comments get out of sync with the code and become misleading
Cluttering the file with useless text

detection_metrics.redundant_comment_ratio: The comment verbatim duplicates the name of a variable or method
detection_metrics.outdated_comments: Comments describe logic that no longer exists

refactoring_techniques.name: Extract Method with Descriptive Name
refactoring_techniques.description: Replacing a commented block with code inside a method with a clear name.

refactoring_techniques.name: Rename Variable / Function
refactoring_techniques.description: Giving variables and functions self-documenting names.

bad_example.explanation: Obscure abbreviations `u.st`, `u.tp`, `u.reg`, `u.a` are masked by a comment above.

good_example.code:
if user.is_eligible_for_eu_premium_service():
    charge_fee(user)
good_example.explanation: The code has become self-documenting. An additional comment is no longer required.

smells.name: Redundant Wrapper / Pass-Through
smells.summary: A method or function that merely forwards a call to an internal object without changes, adding no value.
smells.definition: A code smell where a wrapper method is created whose sole purpose is to pass all received parameters one-to-one to an underlying method. Often arises from poor facade design or residual architectural layers.
symptoms: The method body consists of a single line `return this.underlyingService.do(a, b, c);`
Dozens of twin methods in a controller/service that perform no validation or transformation
root_causes: Blind creation of intermediate service layers 'by template' where they are not needed
Fear of accessing the repository directly from a simple scenario
impact: Maintenance overhead for meaningless intermediate call levels
Increased call stack depth

detection_metrics.one_liner_delegates: The method consists of 1 line directly forwarding the call to another field

refactoring_techniques.name: Remove Middle Man / Inline Method
refactoring_techniques.description: Removing the middleman and accessing the target object directly.

bad_example.explanation: The controller method does absolutely nothing except mechanically forwarding the call.

good_example.explanation: The controller has gained real responsibility (validating HTTP request parameters and formatting the HTTP response).

smells.name: Feature Envy
smells.summary: A method accesses the data and methods of another object more frequently than its own class's fields and methods.
smells.definition: A classic code smell formulated by Martin Fowler. A method of class A continuously queries the fields or getters of an object of class B to perform calculations. This is a clear signal that the method is 'in the wrong class' and should be moved inside class B.
symptoms: The method constantly calls getters of the same parameter object
The current class's own fields are not used at all in the method body
Calculations are performed on foreign data on the client side
root_causes: Separation of data and behavior (gravitation toward procedural style)
Reluctance to extend a third-party DTO class with useful behavior
impact: Violation of the High Cohesion principle
Increased coupling between classes

detection_metrics.foreign_access_ratio: > 60% of data accesses in the method are directed to a single external object
detection_metrics.self_field_access: 0 accesses to fields of its own class

refactoring_techniques.name: Move Method
refactoring_techniques.description: Moving the entire method into the class whose data it manipulates.

refactoring_techniques.name: Extract Method & Move Method
refactoring_techniques.description: Extracting the envious fragment of the method and moving only that part.

bad_example.explanation: The `calculate_discounted_price` method operates entirely on `Order` and `Customer` object data, having no relation to the report generator.

good_example.explanation: The logic has been moved to the `Order` class. Data and behavior are combined in a single object.

smells.name: Inappropriate Intimacy
smells.summary: Classes are too deeply aware of each other's internal implementation details and private data.
smells.definition: A design smell in which two classes know too much about each other: accessing non-public fields, depending on specific internal structures, or mutually calling hidden mechanisms. This destroys encapsulation and makes it impossible to change one class without breaking the other.
symptoms: Frequent use of reflection or the `internal`/`friend` modifier to bypass privacy
Class A directly manipulates a collection inside class B instead of calling semantic methods
Circular dependency between two classes
root_causes: Violation of the Information Hiding principle
Poorly designed API of the partner class
impact: Fragility: changing the internal structure of one class leads to the breakdown of its neighbor
Inability to reuse one class separately from the other

detection_metrics.bidirectional_dependencies: Two classes tightly reference each other's private members or internal types

refactoring_techniques.name: Move Method / Move Field
refactoring_techniques.description: Moving logic so as to reduce intimate dependency.

refactoring_techniques.name: Change Bidirectional Association to Unidirectional
refactoring_techniques.description: Eliminating cyclic coupling and organizing a unidirectional data flow.

refactoring_techniques.name: Encapsulate Collection
refactoring_techniques.description: Prohibiting direct access to internal collections by returning ReadOnly wrappers.

bad_example.explanation: The `CheckoutService` service directly modifies the cart's private structures. If the cart switches its storage to Map or starts accounting for tax, the service will corrupt the data.

good_example.explanation: The cart hides the array inside itself and provides a controlled modification method. Encapsulation is restored.

smells.name: Message Chains
smells.summary: A client requests an object from one object, then requests a third from the received object, forming a long chain of calls.
smells.definition: A code smell consisting of a long series of sequential calls `client.getA().getB().getC().getValue()`. The client ends up tightly coupled to navigating the entire chain of dependencies. Any change in the intermediate classes requires updating the client code.
symptoms: Multiple arrow calls or dots in a row: `user.getOrganization().getDepartment().getHead().getEmail()`
Difficulty when writing tests: the need to prepare a deep tree of mocks
root_causes: Ignoring the Law of Demeter
Lack of methods for hiding intermediate delegation
impact: Any change in the relationship structure between intermediate classes breaks clients
High probability of unexpected NullReferenceException

detection_metrics.chain_length: > 2 consecutive accesses to properties/getters of different classes

refactoring_techniques.name: Hide Delegate
refactoring_techniques.description: Creating a method on the source object that handles the call to the chain.

refactoring_techniques.name: Extract Method & Move Method
refactoring_techniques.description: Moving logic to the final consumer of the chain.

bad_example.explanation: The client is tightly coupled to the fact that a company is divided into branches, and a branch has a manager.

good_example.explanation: The `User` class encapsulates the details of finding a manager. The client does not know about and does not depend on the internal structure of the company.

smells.name: Middle Man
smells.summary: A class delegates the vast majority of its responsibilities to another class, performing only empty delegation.
smells.definition: A code smell that is the opposite of the Message Chains smell. It occurs when, in an attempt to hide delegation, developers go too far: class A contains dozens of methods that do nothing but call methods with the same name on class B. Class A turns into a useless 'middle man'.
symptoms: More than half of the class's methods are trivial delegates to a single field
When adding a new method to class B, it must be mechanically duplicated in class A
root_causes: Excessive delegation hiding
Architecture erosion after the removal of the class's own logic
impact: Cluttering the system with useless layers and redundant code
Difficulty navigating calls in the debugger

detection_metrics.delegation_methods_ratio: > 50% of class methods simply call a similar method of an internal object

refactoring_techniques.name: Remove Middle Man
refactoring_techniques.description: Providing direct access to the internal object or eliminating the middle man class.

refactoring_techniques.name: Inline Method
refactoring_techniques.description: Inlining the delegating method into the call site.

bad_example.explanation: The `Person` class carries no useful functionality with respect to the department, but merely mechanically duplicates the methods of the `Department` class.

good_example.explanation: The middle man is eliminated. The client accesses the `Department` object directly.

smells.name: Insider Trading
smells.summary: Two or more modules exchange private data bypassing public contracts and architectural conventions.
smells.definition: A design smell where modules or packages that should be isolated covertly exchange non-public information by looking into each other's files or using closed internal channels. This invisibly binds modules with a web of hidden dependencies.
symptoms: Importing private files or undocumented internal structures of a neighboring package
Using shared global mutable variables to exchange information between services
root_causes: Quick 'hacks' for the sake of an urgent defect fix
Lack of a formalized public API between subsystems
impact: Inability to update or replace one module in isolation without breaking its neighbor
Hard-to-track side effects

detection_metrics.private_import_violations: Imports from `/internal/` or `_private` directories of other modules

refactoring_techniques.name: Move Method / Move Field
refactoring_techniques.description: Moving shared data to a third independent intermediary module.

refactoring_techniques.name: Extract Shared Library
refactoring_techniques.description: Creating a separate contract or a public DTO.

bad_example.explanation: The `Billing` module uses an undocumented internal function of the `Analytics` module, breaking the boundary between subsystems.

good_example.explanation: The modules are isolated by a public contract. The internal implementation of the `Analytics` module is free to change.

smells.name: Incomplete Library Class
smells.summary: A third-party library or class does not provide a critically needed method, and the logic compensating for this deficiency is duplicated across the codebase.
smells.definition: A code smell that occurs when an external dependency (library) does not contain a needed helper method (for example, a date format validation or currency conversion function), and developers start copying identical helpers into different parts of the project instead of creating a centralized extension.
symptoms: Scattered utility functions operating on the same library data type
Duplication of micro-conversions before calling library methods
root_causes: Inability to directly modify the source code of an external library
Lack of a centralized integration layer for third-party libraries
impact: Duplication of integration code
Divergent implementations of the same missing functionality in different parts of the project

detection_metrics.library_helper_duplicates: Repetition of similar wrapper functions over a library type in >= 3 files

refactoring_techniques.name: Introduce Foreign Method
refactoring_techniques.description: Creating an extension method (Extension Method) for the library type.

refactoring_techniques.name: Introduce Local Extension (Subclass / Wrapper)
refactoring_techniques.description: Creating a subclass or a wrapper around the library class with all the necessary methods.

bad_example.explanation: The missing method of an external library is manually implemented and duplicated in multiple places with potential discrepancies.

good_example.explanation: The library class is extended with a clean extension method available centrally to the entire project.

smells.name: Hidden Side Effects
smells.summary: A function performs unexpected modifications of external state or I/O that are not stated in its name and signature.
smells.definition: A code smell that violates the Command-Query Separation (CQS) principle. A function declared as a pure query or check (for example, `isValidUser` or `calculateTotal`) covertly modifies a database record, resets a session token, or sends a network request. A developer calling the function for validation purposes unintentionally mutates the system state.
symptoms: Methods `isX()`, `checkY()`, `getZ()` write to the database or modify the state of global variables
Calling the method in a test leads to unexpected side effects (for example, file creation or debiting money)
Repeated call to the function with the same arguments returns a different result (non-idempotency)
root_causes: Violation of the Command-Query Separation (CQS) principle
Desire to optimize code by 'performing another action along the way'
Poor function names
impact: Extremely hard-to-track bugs occurring during innocent condition checks
Inability to safely call the method from concurrent threads

detection_metrics.cqs_violations: Methods returning a boolean value or data contain INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE/I-O operations

refactoring_techniques.name: Separate Query from Modifier
refactoring_techniques.description: Splitting the function into two: a pure query without side effects and an explicit modifier command.

refactoring_techniques.name: Rename Method
refactoring_techniques.description: Reflecting the actual side effect in the method name if separation is not possible.

bad_example.explanation: The function is named `checkUserPassword` (password check), but on success covertly updates the session token and rewrites the user in the database. Calling this check in a validator will break the user's current session.

good_example.explanation: The query is separated from the command. The password check has become pure and safe for repeated calls.

smells.name: Mutating Input Arguments
smells.summary: A function modifies an argument passed to it (an object or array), violating the caller's expectations.
smells.definition: A code smell in which a function does not return a new modified object, but mutates the passed data structure by reference (in-place mutation). As a result, the external code that owns this object encounters an unexpected change in its internal state, leading to elusive defects.
symptoms: The function sorts the passed array in place (`array.sort()`) instead of returning a copy
Fields of the passed DTO are overwritten inside an auxiliary service
Reusing the passed argument after calling the function leads to a failure
root_causes: Procedural programming habits
Misconception about memory optimization by avoiding the creation of new objects
impact: Violation of the immutability principle (Immutability)
Unpredictable data races in multithreaded or asynchronous code

detection_metrics.param_mutation_rate: Reassigning properties or elements of arguments inside the function body

refactoring_techniques.name: Return New Object
refactoring_techniques.description: Creating and returning a new immutable copy of data with the changes applied.

refactoring_techniques.name: Use Readonly Types
refactoring_techniques.description: Marking parameters as `readonly` or `ReadonlyArray` for protection at compile time.

bad_example.explanation: The calling code passed an `items` array, and its prices were unpredictably decreased. If the function is called twice, the discount is applied twice.

good_example.explanation: The function has become pure: input parameters are protected with the `readonly` modifier, and the result is returned as a new immutable array.

smells.name: Deeply Nested Control Flow / Arrow Anti-Pattern
smells.name_en: Deeply Nested Control Flow / Arrow Anti-Pattern
smells.summary: Multiple nested if/else blocks, loops, and try/catch blocks forming an indentation 'arrow'.
smells.definition: A code smell where method logic drifts to the right across 4-6 indentation levels due to sequential condition checks. This turns code reading into a difficult task, as the developer must simultaneously keep the context of all enclosing conditions in mind.
symptoms: The code visually resembles an arrowhead `>` due to indentation
More than 3 levels of nesting for constructs (`if`, `for`, `try`, `while`)
Closing curly braces take up half the screen at the end of the function
root_causes: Positive branching (deferring error handling until the very end)
Lack of knowledge of the early return pattern (Guard Clauses / Return Early)
impact: High cyclomatic and cognitive complexity
Extremely easy omission of edge cases during testing

refactoring_techniques.name: Replace Nested Conditional with Guard Clauses (Replacing Conditionals with Guard Clauses)
refactoring_techniques.description: Checking negative conditions at the beginning of the method with an immediate exit (`return` / `throw`).

refactoring_techniques.name: Extract Method
refactoring_techniques.description: Extracting inner loop bodies and branches into separate methods.

bad_example.explanation: Arrow anti-pattern: useful business logic is hidden at the 5th level of nesting, while errors are scattered at the bottom.

good_example.code:
def process_payment(user, payment_info):
    # Защитные условия (Guard Clauses) с ранним выходом:
    if user is None: return "Пользователь не найден"
    if not user.is_active: return "Пользователь заблокирован"
    if payment_info is None: return "Нет платежных данных"
    if payment_info.amount <= 0: return "Некорректная сумма"
    if not user.has_funds(payment_info.amount): return "Недостаточно средств"

    # Основной сценарий идет на верхнем уровне:
    return execute_transaction(user, payment_info)
good_example.explanation: The code has become flat and linear. Each check immediately terminates execution in case of an error, and the happy path is easy to read.

smells.name: Flag Argument
smells.summary: Passing a boolean flag into a method to switch its internal execution logic.
smells.definition: A code smell described by Robert Martin. Passing a boolean parameter (for example, `render(true)` or `createInvoice(isVip: boolean)`) means that the method does two fundamentally different things depending on the flag value. The method violates SRP and impairs code readability at the call site.
symptoms: The function call looks cryptic: `processOrder(order, true, false)`
Inside the method, the first thing that happens is `if (flag) { ... } else { ... }`
Parameter documentation explains: 'if true, does A, otherwise does B'
root_causes: Desire to combine two similar functions into a single 'universal' one
Reluctance to create two explicit methods with clear names
impact: Unreadable call sites (Boolean Literal Smell)
Violation of the Single Responsibility Principle

detection_metrics.boolean_parameters_count: >= 1 boolean argument that determines the execution flow within the method body

refactoring_techniques.name: Decompose Method into Two (Splitting a Method into Two)
refactoring_techniques.description: Creating two separate methods with self-explanatory names instead of a single flag-based method.

refactoring_techniques.name: Replace Parameter with Named Enum
refactoring_techniques.description: Using an explicit Enum or options object instead of a mute boolean.

bad_example.explanation: The call `exportReport(true)` forces the developer to inspect the function declaration to understand what `true` means.

good_example.explanation: The method is split into two specialized ones. The names clearly reflect the action being performed.

smells.name: Output Parameters
smells.summary: Using method parameters to return calculation results (via out, ref, pointers, or argument mutation).
smells.definition: A code smell where a method returns results not via the standard `return` value, but by mutating passed arguments (for example, `out`/`ref` keywords in C#, pointers in Go/C++, or passing an empty object to populate). This is counterintuitive for code comprehension, where parameters are meant for input, not output.
symptoms: Using `out` or `ref` in C# to return multiple values
Passing an empty array/object `results` into a method, which the function populates from the inside
Caller code must declare dummy variables prior to invocation
root_causes: Limitations of older language versions that lacked support for returning tuples (Tuples)
An attempt to return execution status and the data itself at the same time
impact: Difficulty reading signatures: it is unclear which parameters are inputs and which are outputs
Inability to conveniently chain method calls

detection_metrics.out_ref_parameters: Presence of parameters with an out/ref modifier in the signature

refactoring_techniques.name: Return Object / Record / Tuple
refactoring_techniques.description: Returning a composite object, tuple, or record via the return statement.

refactoring_techniques.name: Use Result Pattern
refactoring_techniques.description: Applying the Result/Either pattern to return both status and value.

bad_example.explanation: Using `out` keywords complicates calling and testing the function.

good_example.explanation: The function returns a typed `StatsResult` object via `return`, making the signature natural and clean.

smells.name: Premature Optimization
smells.summary: Complicating code with low-level tricks and manual micro-optimizations without profiler confirmation of bottlenecks.
smells.definition: An anti-pattern made famous by Donald Knuth's quote: 'Premature optimization is the root of all evil in programming'. A developer replaces a simple and clear algorithm with complex bit shifts, custom object pools, or obscure data structures where only 10 operations per day are executed.
symptoms: The code is written in a complex, esoteric manner (bit masks, manual inline assembly, replacing standard collections with complex custom ones)
Absence of benchmarks or profiling reports confirming a performance issue
Difficulty in modifying and debugging the algorithm
root_causes: A developer's false assumption about where exactly the system will slow down
A desire to show off knowledge of low-level optimizations
impact: A huge number of elusive bugs
Loss of readability and a sharp increase in code maintenance costs

detection_metrics.manual_bit_twiddling: Use of low-level bitwise operations in business logic

refactoring_techniques.name: Replace Algorithm with Simple Readable Code
refactoring_techniques.description: Reverting to standard readable algorithms and language collections.

refactoring_techniques.name: Profile Before Optimizing
refactoring_techniques.description: Introducing measurements and profiling before making changes.

bad_example.explanation: A bitwise trick in a web application degrades readability for the sake of non-existent nanosecond savings.

good_example.explanation: Simple, expressive, and standard code that is understandable to any developer and well-optimized by the JIT compiler.

smells.name: Magic Numbers and Strings
smells.summary: Using number and string literals directly in formulas and conditions without naming their meaning with constants.
smells.definition: A code smell in which algorithms use obscure constants: numbers (`86400`, `1.18`, `42`) or strings (`"PENDING_AUTH_STEP_2"`), whose meaning is only clear to the author at the time of writing. When such literals are repeated, replacing a value turns into a nightmare.
symptoms: Numeric literals in formulas without explaining their physical or financial meaning
Identical status strings are scattered as literals across multiple files
A typo in a single string literal breaks logic without compilation errors
root_causes: Quick prototyping 'in place'
Reluctance to create enums (Enums) or constant files
impact: Incomprehensibility of formulas: what does the number 86400 or 0.05 mean?
The risk of missing the modification of one of the instances of a number when a business rule changes

detection_metrics.raw_literals_in_expressions: Use of non-canonical numbers (other than 0, 1) in arithmetic or conditions

refactoring_techniques.name: Replace Magic Number with Symbolic Constant
refactoring_techniques.description: Declaring a named constant with a self-explanatory name.

refactoring_techniques.name: Replace String Literal with Enum
refactoring_techniques.description: Replacing string tags with strict enums.

bad_example.explanation: The numbers `299792458` and `86400` are magic constants.

good_example.explanation: Named constants make formulas self-documenting and clear.

smells.name: Temporal Coupling
smells.summary: Class methods must strictly be called in a specific sequence, but this contract is not enforced by anything.
smells.definition: A design smell where method B will fail with an error or return incorrect data if method A was not called before it (for example, `init()`, then `configure()`, then `execute()`). Since the compiler does not enforce the correct order, developers regularly forget to call an intermediate step, resulting in runtime errors.
symptoms: The need to call the `init()` method before any use of the object
`IllegalStateException` exceptions when the call order is not respected
Comments in code: '// WARNING: be sure to call step1() before step2()!'
root_causes: Mutable object lifecycle
Incomplete initialization in the constructor
impact: Occurrence of bugs at runtime due to forgotten preparation calls
Inability to express valid state guarantees in the type system

detection_metrics.init_methods_count: Presence of public init/setup/prepare methods required before worker methods

refactoring_techniques.name: Builder Pattern with Fluent Interface
refactoring_techniques.description: Using a builder with step-by-step types (Step Builder), where the next method is accessible only after the previous one.

refactoring_techniques.name: Constructor Initialization
refactoring_techniques.description: Moving all necessary configuration into constructor parameters.

bad_example.explanation: Client code can accidentally call `generate()` before `setTitle()`, leading to an abnormal program termination.

good_example.explanation: The object is always created valid. Temporal coupling has been eliminated — calling the `generate()` method in an invalid state is now physically impossible.

smells.name: Swallowing Exceptions / Empty Catch Block
smells.summary: Catching an exception with an empty catch block body or without any logging and handling.
smells.definition: One of the most harmful code smells. A `try/catch` block catches an error and does nothing: the `catch` body is empty or contains only an `// ignore` comment. As a result, the system transitions into an inconsistent state, data is silently corrupted, and developers are deprived of the ability to diagnose the cause of the problem.
symptoms: Empty `catch (e) {}` blocks in the codebase
Application failures occur without a trace, without a single line in the logs
The function terminates silently, returning `undefined` or incomplete data structures
root_causes: Desire to silence an error during quick debugging, followed by forgetting about it
Lack of understanding of how to properly handle specific failures
Annoyance with checked exceptions in Java
impact: Inability to localize and debug bugs in production
Silent database corruption and hidden leaks

detection_metrics.empty_catch_count: > 0 empty catch blocks without logging or rethrowing
