refactoring_techniques.name: Log and Handle Appropriately
refactoring_techniques.description: Writing detailed failure context to a logger with ERROR level.

refactoring_techniques.name: Rethrow Wrapped Domain Exception
refactoring_techniques.description: Wrapping in a domain exception while preserving the original cause (Inner Exception).

refactoring_techniques.name: Fallback Gracefully
refactoring_techniques.description: Explicitly switching to a fallback algorithm while recording the event in metrics.

bad_example.explanation: When the database connection drops, the error is ignored. The user thinks the data has been saved, even though it was lost.

good_example.explanation: The error is logged with context and wrapped in a domain exception while preserving the root cause (`cause: error`).

smells.name: Catching Generic Exception
smells.summary: Catching the topmost base exception type (Exception, Throwable, BaseException) instead of specific expected errors.
smells.definition: A code smell where a `catch` block is configured for a generic `Exception` (or worse, `Throwable` in Java), catching not only expected business I/O errors, but also critical system failures (OutOfMemoryError, NullPointerException, ThreadDeath, syntax errors), masking them as ordinary failures.
symptoms: `catch (Exception ex)` or `except Exception:` blocks in Python around large chunks of code
Typo errors in code (for example, accessing a non-existent property) are caught as a 'server connection error'
root_causes: Developer laziness in figuring out exactly which exceptions the called API can throw
An attempt to prevent the application from crashing at all costs
impact: Masking system bugs and memory failures as ordinary business logic errors
Difficulty in localizing critical defects

detection_metrics.generic_catch_count: Usage of catch(Throwable) or catch(Exception) at the application level

refactoring_techniques.name: Catch Specific Exceptions
refactoring_techniques.description: Catching only those specific exception types that can actually be handled.

refactoring_techniques.name: Top-Level Global Exception Handler
refactoring_techniques.description: Leaving the catching of generic Exception only at the topmost framework level.

bad_example.explanation: If the `'settings'` key is missing from the JSON or a memory error occurred, the function will silently return an empty dictionary, masking the bug.

good_example.explanation: Only expected errors are handled (file not found), while file syntax errors are retransmitted upstream with a clear description.

smells.name: Throwing Generic Exception
smells.summary: Throwing a base error type (throw new Exception(), raise Exception()) without using specialized domain classes.
smells.definition: A code smell where a developer generates an exception of the most generic class `Exception` or `Error`. In this case, the calling code is deprived of the ability to selectively catch this error via `catch (PaymentDeclinedException)` and is forced to either catch all exceptions indiscriminately or parse the error message text.
symptoms: Lines like `throw new Exception("Something went wrong");` or `raise Exception(...)`
The calling code checks `if (ex.Message.Contains("not found"))`
root_causes: Laziness to create an exception subclass
Neglecting domain error design
impact: Inability to selectively handle errors in higher layers
Fragile parsing of string error messages

detection_metrics.raw_exception_instantiations: Instantiating the base Exception class in throw statements

refactoring_techniques.name: Create Custom Domain Exception Class
refactoring_techniques.description: Creating a specialized exception class with typed context fields.

bad_example.explanation: The client cannot determine the failure type programmatically other than by comparing the error string.

good_example.explanation: A clear, typed domain exception with machine-readable error data is thrown.

smells.name: Destructive Re-throw (Losing Stack Trace)
smells.summary: Rethrowing an exception via 'throw ex;' or 'raise e', leading to a complete overwrite of the call stack and loss of the original failure location.
smells.definition: A code smell in C#, Java, Python, or JS where a caught exception is rethrown with the loss of the original stack. For example, in C#, the construct `throw ex;` instead of `throw;` resets the StackTrace to the current line, making it impossible to determine exactly where deep inside the library the error occurred.
symptoms: Using `throw ex;` in a `catch (Exception ex)` block in C#
In JS/TS: `catch (e) { throw new Error(e.message); }` without specifying `{ cause: e }`
The stack trace in logs cuts off at the catch block
root_causes: Lack of knowledge of language runtime nuances (the difference between `throw;` and `throw ex;`)
impact: Complete loss of information about the true source of the error during incident investigation

detection_metrics.rethrow_with_variable: Presence of `throw ex;` in C# or creating a new Error without cause in JS

refactoring_techniques.name: Use Parameterless Throw / Cause Chaining
refactoring_techniques.description: Using native `throw;` in C# or the `cause` chain in ES2022+ / Python `from e`.

bad_example.explanation: The `throw ex;` statement overwrites the call stack, destroying information about the actual failing line in `_apiClient`.

good_example.explanation: A clean call to `throw;` preserves the original stack trace chain all the way down to the low-level socket.

smells.name: Log and Throw / Redundant Logging
smells.summary: Writing an error to the logger at each intermediate catch level, followed by rethrowing the same exception.
smells.definition: An error handling anti-pattern: each architectural layer (repository, service, controller) catches an exception, writes it to the log (`logger.error(...)`), and then performs a `throw`. As a result, the same error is duplicated 4-5 times in the log journal with giant walls of stack traces, cluttering the monitoring system.
symptoms: When a single error occurs, 3-5 identical error messages from different classes appear in the logging system
Pollution of logs with duplicate call stacks
root_causes: The golden rule of error handling is violated: 'Either handle and log, or rethrow upward, but do not do both at the same time'
impact: Bloating log volume and distorting alerting metrics (a single failure generates 5 alerts)
Difficulty reading incident logs

detection_metrics.log_then_rethrow_pattern: Calling an Error-level logger immediately before a throw statement within the same catch block

refactoring_techniques.name: Log Once at Boundary
refactoring_techniques.description: Logging the exception only once at the external boundary of the system (Global Exception Filter).

bad_example.explanation: The exact same error with an identical stack trace is written to the log three times.

good_example.explanation: The error is logged exactly once at the boundary of the system with full context.

smells.name: Exception as Flow Control
smells.summary: Using an exception mechanism instead of standard if/else conditional operators for routine logic branching.
smells.definition: A design anti-pattern where expected routine situations (for example, 'user not found', 'end of file reached', 'invalid form input') are handled by throwing and catching exceptions. Throwing exceptions is extremely slow (building a stack trace consumes milliseconds) and turns code into something resembling convoluted `goto` jumps.
symptoms: An exception is thrown in an expected normal system operation scenario
The `catch` body contains regular business logic ('if not found in cache — fetch from DB')
Performance degradation in heavy loops
root_causes: Reluctance to use `Optional`, `Result` types, or explicit checks
impact: Colossal performance degradation (instantiating an exception is hundreds of times slower than a simple if)
Inability to debug with the 'Break on all exceptions' option enabled

detection_metrics.expected_exception_rate: Throwing exceptions during regular routine user requests

refactoring_techniques.name: Replace Exception with Precheck (Test Before Calling)
refactoring_techniques.description: Checking a condition via if before invoking a method instead of catching an error.

refactoring_techniques.name: Use Result / Optional Pattern
refactoring_techniques.description: Returning a Result object with the operation result instead of throwing an exception.

bad_example.explanation: The absence of an element in a list is a routine situation turned into throwing an exception.

good_example.explanation: Clean linear search without exception creation or stack overhead.

smells.name: Returning Null on Failure
smells.summary: A method returns null in case of error or missing data, forcing all calling code to write null checks.
smells.definition: A code smell described by Tony Hoare (the creator of null, who called it his 'billion-dollar mistake'). Returning `null` on error leads to the spread of a 'null-check infection': calling code either forgets to check the result and crashes with a NullReferenceException, or becomes cluttered with dozens of `if (res != null)`.
symptoms: Multiple `if (x == null)` checks across the entire call chain
Application crashes with `NullPointerException` / `Cannot read properties of null` errors
root_causes: Lack of a culture of using Optional/Result types in the project
impact: High fragility of code in production
Loss of information about the cause of failure (null does not explain why the operation failed)

detection_metrics.null_returns_count: Returning the null literal from methods when failures occur

refactoring_techniques.name: Introduce Null Object Pattern
refactoring_techniques.description: Returning a special neutral object with empty behavior.

refactoring_techniques.name: Return Optional / Maybe / Result
refactoring_techniques.description: Explicitly specifying the possible absence of a value in the type system.

bad_example.explanation: Returning `null` conceals why the client is missing (invalid ID or absence in the database) and triggers program crashes when accessing properties.

good_example.explanation: The Result pattern forces the calling code to explicitly handle failure scenarios and clearly explains the cause of the failure.

smells.name: Busy Waiting / Polling Spinlock
smells.summary: Cyclically polling a condition in a tight loop (while), burning 100% of CPU resources.
smells.definition: A multithreaded code smell where a thread waits for an event to occur or a resource to be released in an empty loop `while (!ready) {}` without going to sleep or using system wait primitives (ManualResetEvent, Monitor, Semaphore, Future/Promise). This leads to instantaneous 100% CPU core utilization and processor heating.
symptoms: A tight `while (!flag)` or `while (queue.isEmpty())` loop
Utilization of one or more CPU cores at 100% during system idle state
Battery drain on mobile and portable devices
root_causes: Lack of knowledge of thread synchronization primitives (Condition Variables, Wait/Notify, Channels)
An attempt to avoid OS context switching overhead
impact: Senseless burning of processor time and energy
Starvation of other threads (Thread Starvation) that do not receive a time slice

detection_metrics.empty_while_loops: while/for loops with an empty body or without yield/wait/sleep calls

refactoring_techniques.name: Use Synchronization Primitives (Wait/Notify, ManualResetEvent)
refactoring_techniques.description: Putting the waiting thread into OS kernel sleep mode until an explicit signal is received.

refactoring_techniques.name: Use Async/Await or Blocking Queues
refactoring_techniques.description: Using asynchronous tasks or blocking queues (BlockingQueue).

bad_example.explanation: The thread spins in an infinite loop, utilizing a CPU core at full capacity and interfering with other tasks.

good_example.explanation: `TaskCompletionSource` is used. The thread is released back to the pool and does not consume CPU resources while waiting.

smells.name: Unprotected Shared State / Race Hazard
smells.summary: Concurrent access of multiple threads to shared mutable data without synchronization or atomic operations.
smells.definition: A critical multithreading smell. Multiple threads concurrently read and modify a shared collection, counter variable, or object without using mutexes, locks, or atomic primitives. This leads to a race condition (Race Condition), lost updates, and memory corruption.
symptoms: Intermittent errors: the resulting counter `counter++` in 10 threads is less than 10 000
`ConcurrentModificationException` exceptions in Java or dictionary corruption in .NET
Bugs are reproducible only under load and disappear during step-by-step debugging (Heisenbug)
root_causes: Lack of understanding that operations like `i++` are not atomic at the processor level
Using standard collections (List, Dictionary) instead of thread-safe ones
impact: Unpredictable data corruption and financial discrepancies
Runtime crashes at random points in time

detection_metrics.thread_sanitizer_warnings: Race detection by ThreadSanitizer or SonarQube tools
detection_metrics.non_thread_safe_collections_in_singleton: Using standard List/Map in fields of singleton services

refactoring_techniques.name: Use Atomic Primitives (AtomicInteger, Interlocked)
refactoring_techniques.description: Using hardware CAS (Compare-And-Swap) instructions for primitives.

refactoring_techniques.name: Use Concurrent Collections
refactoring_techniques.description: Replacing collections with ConcurrentDictionary, CopyOnWriteArrayList, etc.

refactoring_techniques.name: Immutability & Message Passing
refactoring_techniques.description: Transitioning to immutable data and message passing via channels (Actor Model).

bad_example.explanation: When calling `increment()` from 100 parallel threads, the resulting value will randomly be less than 100 due to overwriting of CPU registers.

good_example.explanation: `AtomicInteger` is used, guaranteeing the correctness of data updates at the processor instruction level.

smells.name: Broken Double-Checked Locking
smells.summary: An attempt to optimize singleton creation using a double check for null without the volatile modifier or memory barriers.
smells.definition: A classic multithreading defect in Java and C++. The developer attempts to avoid synchronization overhead during lazy initialization by checking `instance == null` before and after entering the `lock` block. Without specifying the `volatile` modifier, the compiler or processor can reorder write instructions, causing another thread to observe a partially initialized object.
symptoms: Rare crashes with NullPointerException or reading default field values in multithreaded tests
Object initialization is visible to other threads before its constructor completes execution
root_causes: Processor instruction reordering (Instruction Reordering) and caches in CPU cores
impact: Extremely rare but fatal failures during service initialization under load

detection_metrics.dcl_without_volatile: Double check for null on a field without the volatile keyword

refactoring_techniques.name: Use Volatile Modifier
refactoring_techniques.description: Declaring the reference with the volatile keyword to establish a memory barrier.

refactoring_techniques.name: Use Language Lazy Primitives
refactoring_techniques.description: Using built-in thread-safe wrappers (`Lazy<T>` in .NET or Initialization-on-demand holder in Java).

bad_example.explanation: Without `volatile` or `Lazy<T>`, another thread can read the `_instance` reference before the constructor finishes populating the object's internal fields.

good_example.explanation: Standard `Lazy<T>` is used, guaranteeing correct memory barriers and thread safety at the runtime level.

smells.name: Blocking Async Code / Sync over Async
smells.name_en: Blocking Async Code / Sync over Async
smells.summary: Blocking wait on an asynchronous task via .Result, .Wait(), or GetAwaiter().GetResult(), causing deadlocks and thread starvation.
smells.definition: A severe antipattern in ecosystems with asynchronous I/O (C#, JS, Python asyncio, Java CompletableFuture). Instead of using `await` end-to-end, the developer calls synchronous waiting via `.Result` or `.Wait()`. In environments with a synchronization context (UI, classic ASP.NET), this is guaranteed to lead to a deadlock (Deadlock), while on the backend it exhausts the thread pool (Thread Pool Starvation).
symptoms: `task.Result`, `task.Wait()`, `task.GetAwaiter().GetResult()` constructs in code
Complete freezing of a web request or UI when accessing a database
Latency increase under load due to queues in ThreadPool
root_causes: Attempting to call an asynchronous method from a synchronous interface without changing the signature
Lack of understanding of the 'Async all the way down' principle
impact: Thread deadlocks (Deadlocks)
Catastrophic drop in web server scalability

detection_metrics.sync_wait_on_task: Calls to .Result / .Wait() / .GetAwaiter().GetResult() on Task / Promise objects

refactoring_techniques.name: Async All the Way
refactoring_techniques.description: End-to-end use of async/await from the controller/entry point down to the database.

bad_example.explanation: Calling `.Result` blocks a system pool thread until the network call completes, destroying all benefits of asynchrony.

good_example.explanation: The controller method has become asynchronous (`async Task`). The thread is returned to the pool during the network wait.

smells.name: Uncontrolled Fire-and-Forget
smells.summary: Launching a background asynchronous task without waiting (await) and without catching potential failure errors.
smells.definition: An asynchronous programming smell (in JS, C#, Python). A task is launched without `await` or without retaining a reference to the Promise/Task. If an error occurs inside this background operation, it turns into an Unhandled Promise Rejection or UnobservedTaskException, which in modern versions of Node.js and .NET can lead to a crash of the entire application process.
symptoms: Calling an asynchronous function without the `await` keyword (`sendEmailAsync(user);`)
Compiler warnings 'Because this call is not awaited, execution of the current method continues...'
Server process crash with an `UnhandledPromiseRejection` error
root_causes: The desire to respond faster to the user in an HTTP request by offloading heavy work 'to the background'
Reluctance to set up a full-fledged background task queue (Celery, Hangfire, BullMQ)
impact: Sudden crash of the entire application upon an error in an unattached promise
Data loss upon server restart (the task is interrupted halfway through)

detection_metrics.task_run_without_await: Task.Run calls without retaining a reference and without exception handling

refactoring_techniques.name: Background Task Queue
refactoring_techniques.description: Moving background processing to a persistent task queue with guaranteed delivery.

refactoring_techniques.name: Attach Global Error Boundary
refactoring_techniques.description: Explicitly attaching an error handler `.catch(err => logger.error(err))`.

bad_example.explanation: If the mail server is unavailable, the thrown error will become an Unhandled Rejection and terminate the Node.js process.

good_example.explanation: The email sending task is placed in a reliable queue with retries on failure and isolation from the HTTP request processing pipeline.

smells.name: Non-Thread-Safe Singleton / Mutable Global State
smells.summary: A singleton stores mutable instance state that is concurrently accessed by different request threads.
smells.definition: A design smell in server-side applications (Spring, ASP.NET Core, NestJS) where services are created as Singleton by default. If such a service contains regular fields for storing current user context or intermediate data, requests from concurrent clients begin overwriting each other's data.
symptoms: The service has Singleton scope, but contains mutable fields `currentUser`, `requestStartTime`
One user in the browser suddenly sees another user's profile data
Unpredictable session failures under load
root_causes: Lack of understanding of the difference between Singleton and Scoped / Transient lifecycles in DI containers
impact: Critical leakage of confidential data between users
Corruption of financial and personal information

detection_metrics.mutable_fields_in_singleton: Presence of mutable non-static fields in classes annotated with @Singleton / @Service

refactoring_techniques.name: Change Lifetime to Scoped
refactoring_techniques.description: Changing the service lifetime in DI to Scoped (for the duration of a single request).

refactoring_techniques.name: Make Singleton Stateless
refactoring_techniques.description: Eliminating mutable fields from the service; passing context via method arguments.

bad_example.explanation: When two users make concurrent requests, `currentUserId` will be overwritten, and the confirmation will be sent to the wrong client.

good_example.explanation: The service has no mutable state. All data is passed through method arguments, making it 100% thread-safe.

smells.name: God Object / Architectural Hub
smells.summary: A central hub or monolithic module of the system on which almost all other components depend and which knows about everything.
smells.definition: A macro-architecture antipattern where an 'uber-component' forms in the system (for example, `AppCore`, `MasterEngine`, or `SystemContext`), where dependencies of hundreds of modules converge. Any change in this node causes a cascading rebuild and a risk of breaking the entire application.
symptoms: The system's dependency graph looks like a hub-and-spoke wheel: all arrows point to a single module
Project compilation/build time increases sharply due to the impossibility of incremental builds
The module contains thousands of lines of heterogeneous code and dozens of subfolders
root_causes: Lack of architectural oversight and boundaries between bounded contexts (Bounded Contexts)
Dumping any new shared code into a `Common` / `Core` / `Utils` folder
impact: Complete paralysis of parallel development by multiple teams
Inability to extract independent services or microservices

detection_metrics.afferent_coupling_ca: Extremely high afferent coupling (Ca > 50 dependent modules)
detection_metrics.hub_centrality: High centrality score in the dependency graph

refactoring_techniques.name: Modular Decomposition by Bounded Context
refactoring_techniques.description: Decomposing the system into independent domain modules following the DDD methodology.

refactoring_techniques.name: Inversion of Control (Dependency Inversion)
refactoring_techniques.description: Inverting dependency arrows using interfaces.

bad_example.explanation: Any class in the project accepts `CoreKernel` as an argument and has access to absolutely everything, bypassing architectural boundaries.

good_example.explanation: The monolith is decomposed into autonomous, loosely coupled modules that interact via events (Event-Driven Architecture).

smells.name: Spaghetti Code
smells.summary: Tangled application structure with unpredictable cross-calls, lack of clear layers, and chaotic control flow.
smells.definition: An archetypal software engineering antipattern. A codebase lacking any structured concept or architectural style. Functions call each other in circles, global variables are modified from different ends of the application, and presentation layers access device drivers or the database directly.
symptoms: It is impossible to draw an understandable architectural data flow diagram
Every change breaks completely unexpected functionality in another part of the system
A new engineer needs several months just to understand how the program works
root_causes: Years of layered edits without refactoring (accumulated technical debt)
Lack of architectural rule linting in the repository
impact: The project becomes 'unmaintainable' (unfit for maintenance), and the development of new features slows down severalfold
Catastrophic cost of software ownership

detection_metrics.cyclomatic_complexity_density: Extremely high cyclomatic complexity of the entire system

refactoring_techniques.name: Layered / Hexagonal Architecture Refactoring
refactoring_techniques.description: Gradual establishment of clear architectural layers (Domain, Application, Infrastructure).

refactoring_techniques.name: Strangler Fig Pattern (Strangler Pattern)
refactoring_techniques.description: Gradual replacement of the old spaghetti monolith with new clean modules.

bad_example.code:
# В файле UI формы авторизации:
import socket
import sqlite3

def on_login_button_click():
    global CURRENT_SESSION
    # Прямой SQL прямо в обработчике кнопки:
    conn = sqlite3.connect('main.db')
    # Прямой сетевой вызов низкоуровневого сокета:
    s = socket.socket()
    s.connect(('192.168.1.1', 8080))
    # Модификация глобального состояния:
    CURRENT_SESSION = {'user': 'admin', 'socket': s}
bad_example.explanation: The UI component directly manages raw sockets, opens a connection to SQLite, and writes to a global variable. Complete absence of abstractions and layers.

good_example.explanation: The UI delegates the task to an interactor/Use Case, which works through abstract repositories and services without directly accessing the database and sockets.

smells.name: Cyclic Dependencies
smells.summary: Two or more modules depend on each other directly or transitively (A -> B -> C -> A), forming a closed loop.
smells.definition: An architectural smell violating the Acyclic Dependencies Principle (ADP). When module A depends on module B, and B directly or indirectly depends on A, they can no longer be compiled, tested, or deployed separately. In effect, they merge into one inseparable mega-module.
symptoms: Compiler or runtime errors 'Circular dependency detected' / 'ImportError: cannot import name... due to circular import'
Inability to run unit tests of module A without connecting the entire module B
The need to use hacks with deferred imports (dynamic import inside a function)
root_causes: Incorrect distribution of entities across packages
Direct access to implementation details of an adjacent module instead of applying dependency inversion
impact: Issues when building and loading modules in JS/Python/Go
Inability to reuse one module without the other

detection_metrics.dependency_graph_cycles: > 0 cycles in the package dependency graph (detected by utilities `madge`, `jdupes`, `sonarqube`)

refactoring_techniques.name: Apply Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP)
refactoring_techniques.description: Extracting the interface into a separate independent contract package.

refactoring_techniques.name: Extract Shared Component
refactoring_techniques.description: Extracting the entity causing the cycle into a third shared module C (A -> C, B -> C).

bad_example.explanation: The files `Order.ts` and `Customer.ts` cyclically import each other. In modular environments, this leads to receiving `undefined` during early initialization.

good_example.explanation: The cycle is broken thanks to applying the Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP). `Order` no longer imports the `Customer` class.

smells.name: Leaky Abstraction
smells.summary: An abstraction layer reveals internal implementation details of the underlying layer outward to clients.
smells.definition: A design smell based on Joel Spolsky's law: 'All non-trivial abstractions, to some degree, are leaky'. It manifests when an interface or abstract service forces calling code to know about the specifics of a low-level technology (for example, specific SQL errors leaking through an IRepository interface, or HTTP headers in a domain service).
symptoms: A business logic interface accepts types like `SqlDataReader`, `HttpRequest`, or `BsonDocument`
The client has to catch specific database exceptions (`SqlException`) when working with an abstract service
Changing the data provider breaks top-level interfaces
root_causes: Incomplete encapsulation of adapters
Developer laziness in mapping system types to domain models
impact: Pointlessness of the abstraction layer: clients are still tightly coupled to the technology anyway
Difficulty of replacing implementations in tests

detection_metrics.technology_specific_types_in_abstraction: Presence of database/network library types in domain layer interface signatures

refactoring_techniques.name: Translate Exceptions to Domain Errors
refactoring_techniques.description: Catching infrastructure errors and translating them into domain exception types.

refactoring_techniques.name: Use Pure Domain DTOs
refactoring_techniques.description: Complete replacement of third-party library types with pure domain objects.

bad_example.explanation: The `IUserRepository` interface leaks MongoDB details. Replacing the DBMS with PostgreSQL without changing signatures is impossible.

good_example.explanation: The contract is completely isolated from storage details. Mapping BSON to the `User` model occurs inside the repository implementation.

smells.name: Interface Bloat / Fat Interface
smells.summary: An interface contains too many disparate methods, forcing clients to implement unnecessary features.
smells.definition: A design smell that directly violates the Interface Segregation Principle (ISP). The interface includes dozens of methods for reading, writing, auditing, printing, sending email, etc. As a result, clients that only require reading are forced to depend on writing methods or implement them with stubs.
symptoms: Implementing classes contain empty methods or throw `NotSupportedException` for half of the interface methods
The interface contains over 10-15 methods
When adding a new method to the interface, dozens of unrelated implementing classes have to be updated
root_causes: An attempt to create a single universal interface for the entire entity ('one class — one gigantic interface')
Lack of understanding of the Role Interfaces concept
impact: False coupling: modifying a printing method forces recompilation of clients that only need reading
Difficulty of creating mock objects in tests

detection_metrics.stub_implementations: Interface implementations where methods remain empty stubs

refactoring_techniques.name: Segregate Interface into Role Interfaces
refactoring_techniques.description: Splitting a large interface into several narrow role-based contracts.

bad_example.explanation: The `IWorker` interface is bloated and violates ISP. The developer is forced to throw exceptions for budget and cleaning methods.

good_example.explanation: Interfaces are split by role. Classes subscribe only to the contracts they actually support.

smells.name: Architecture Layer Bleed / Layer Violation
smells.summary: Direct access from a high-level layer to low-level details, bypassing architectural rules.
smells.definition: An architecture smell that occurs when higher-level components (Presentation / UI / Controllers) access the lowest layers (Database / ORM / Network Sockets) directly, skipping over the business logic and domain layers. This turns a layered architecture into a fiction.
symptoms: SQL queries, HQL, or LINQ queries to the database are written directly in Web API controller methods
Direct creation of an HTTP client in a domain entity
UI components directly use database entities instead of DTOs
root_causes: The desire to 'quickly build a feature', bypassing services and repositories
Lack of architectural linting (ArchUnit, NetArchTest)
impact: Complete loss of the benefits of layered architecture
Inability to test business logic in isolation from the database and network

detection_metrics.arch_lint_violations: Direct imports of infrastructure packages in UI or Domain layers

refactoring_techniques.name: Enforce Layered Architecture with Linter
refactoring_techniques.description: Introducing automated architecture tests (ArchUnit) that block forbidden imports.

refactoring_techniques.name: Move Logic to Application / Domain Service
refactoring_techniques.description: Moving logic to the appropriate application layer.

bad_example.explanation: The controller takes on the role of a repository and business logic, accessing the database directly, bypassing the service layer.

good_example.explanation: The controller is only responsible for HTTP. Business logic is delegated to the service layer, which works with storage abstractions.

smells.name: Hardcoded Environment Configuration
smells.summary: Server URLs, ports, file paths, and environment settings hardcoded in the source code.
smells.definition: An architecture smell violating the 12-Factor App methodology (Section III. Config). Instead of reading settings from environment variables (`process.env`, `os.environ`), the developer hardcodes constants like `https://api.dev.company.com` directly in code, making it impossible to deploy the same artifact to dev/staging/prod.
symptoms: Strings like `http://localhost:5000` or server IP addresses are hardcoded directly in service code
To switch environments from dev to prod, code must be modified and a new commit created
root_causes: Development 'only for the local machine' without considering CI/CD and containerization requirements
impact: Impossibility of automated deployment to Kubernetes / clouds
Danger of a test environment accidentally accessing the production database

detection_metrics.raw_ips_and_urls_in_code: Regular expressions matching IP addresses and external domains outside configuration files

refactoring_techniques.name: Extract to Environment Variables (12-Factor App)
refactoring_techniques.description: Extracting parameters into environment variables with startup validation (Zod, Pydantic Settings).

bad_example.explanation: The URL and timeout are hardcoded directly into the class. To deploy to production, the source code will have to be manually rewritten.

good_example.explanation: Configuration is read from environment variables. The same container/build can run in any environment without changes.

smells.name: Assertion Roulette
smells.summary: Multiple silent assertions (assert) in a row in a single test without explanatory messages.
smells.definition: A unit test smell described by Gerard Meszaros in 'xUnit Test Patterns'. A test contains 10-15 calls to `assert` or `expect` without explaining the context. When the fifth assert fails in CI, the developer only sees 'expected 42, got 0' without the slightest understanding of which specific business rule broke.
symptoms: A single test contains a long list of `assert` calls
Not a single assert contains a text message describing the criterion being verified
When the very first assert fails, execution is halted, and the status of the remaining checks is unknown
root_causes: An attempt to test all possible scenarios of an object in a single test method
Laziness to write separate tests following the 'One test — one behavior' rule
impact: Increased time to localize defects in CI/CD
Loss of clarity in test run reports

detection_metrics.asserts_per_test_count: > 5 assert calls in a single test without text messages

refactoring_techniques.name: Single Assertion per Concept
refactoring_techniques.description: Splitting the test into multiple narrowly focused tests for specific scenarios.

refactoring_techniques.name: Add Assertion Explanations
refactoring_techniques.description: Adding a third message argument to assert calls (e.g., `assertEquals(expected, actual, "Balance must account for commission")`).

bad_example.code:
def test_order_processing():
    order = process_order(sample_order)
    # Рулетка: если упадет 3-й assert, никто не поймет контекста:
    assert order.status == "PAID"
    assert order.total == 1000
    assert len(order.history) == 2
    assert order.customer_notified is True
    assert order.tax_amount == 180
bad_example.explanation: When `assert len(order.history) == 2` fails, CI will only show `AssertionError: assert 1 == 2`, which gives no understanding of which specific history event is missing.

good_example.explanation: Tests are split by verified concepts with descriptive names and check descriptions.

smells.name: Mystery Guest
smells.summary: The test uses external implicit data (files on disk, a pre-populated database) hidden from the eyes of the test reader.
smells.definition: A unit testing smell where the test is not self-contained: it relies on data located in external sources (a fixture in a shared `test_data.sql` file, a file on a server, or a shared database) created outside of the current test. When reading the test, it is impossible to understand where the magic IDs come from and why this exact value is expected.
symptoms: The test performs `database.find("user_id_482")` without previously creating this record in the test
Tests fail when run on another developer's machine because a specific file `C:\test.txt` is missing there
Tests break each other when shared fixtures are modified
root_causes: Using shared global fixtures (Shared Fixture) to save lines of code
impact: Test fragility and mutual interference between tests
Incomprehensibility of the test: to understand the test, one has to open 5 external files

detection_metrics.implicit_external_dependencies: Usage of hardcoded IDs from a prepopulated external database

refactoring_techniques.name: Use Test Data Builder / Object Mother
refactoring_techniques.description: Creating all necessary entities directly in the Arrange/Given phase of the test using builders.

refactoring_techniques.name: Fresh Fixture
refactoring_techniques.description: Creating an isolated dataset for each individual test.

bad_example.explanation: The reader cannot see the age and status of client #42. If another test modifies this client in the shared database, this test will fail.

good_example.explanation: The test is completely self-contained (Self-Contained Test). The Test Data Builder pattern is applied.

smells.name: Hardcoded Test Data
smells.summary: Manually initializing giant test objects with dozens of irrelevant fields directly in the test body, obscuring the essence of the verification.
smells.definition: A unit testing smell where huge objects with all fields populated (addresses, passports, phone numbers, dates) are manually created in the test code, even though only one field matters for the scenario under test (e.g., age or balance). The test reader is forced to wade through mountains of informational noise, trying to guess which exact parameters determine the outcome of the verification.
symptoms: Data preparation (Arrange phase) takes up more than 70% of the lines in the test
Tests contain real personal data (full names, phone numbers) or copied JSON dumps
When adding a new required field to an entity, hundreds of tests have to be manually edited
root_causes: Absence of data factories and fixture builders with sensible default values
Copying a 'working data example' from other tests
impact: Colossal visual noise: the essence of the business rule being tested cannot be seen behind the trees of fields
Extremely high cost of test maintenance when the structure of domain models changes

detection_metrics.arrange_phase_lines: > 20 lines of manual data structure declaration in a single test

refactoring_techniques.name: Test Data Builder Pattern
refactoring_techniques.description: Creating an entity builder with valid default values that allows explicitly setting only relevant fields.

refactoring_techniques.name: Object Mother Pattern
refactoring_techniques.description: Using factory methods (e.g., `createActiveUser()`, `createVipCustomer()`).

bad_example.explanation: Out of 12 user fields, only `age` matters for the test. The remaining fields create noise and fragility.

good_example.explanation: The test is focused only on the aspect being tested (`withAge(21)`). All other required fields are correctly generated by the builder.

smells.name: Eager Test
smells.summary: A single test checks multiple heterogeneous methods and scenarios of an object at once instead of verifying a single behavior.
smells.definition: A unit testing smell where the developer attempts to test the entire lifecycle of an object in a single test method: creation, profile modification, card binding, password change, and deletion. As a result, the test grows to hundreds of lines, becomes difficult to comprehend, and breaks at the slightest provocation.
symptoms: The test method takes 50-100 lines of code
Inside the test, blocks of calls and assertions alternate: `act() -> assert() -> act() -> assert() -> act()`
It is difficult to come up with a name for the test other than `testUserFlow()` or `testAll()`
root_causes: Perceiving a unit test as a long end-to-end scenario of a manual tester
impact: If the first step fails, subsequent important checks are not even executed
It is impossible to use tests as a behavioral specification (Living Documentation)

detection_metrics.multiple_act_assert_cycles: > 2 alternations of Act-Assert phases in the body of a single test method

refactoring_techniques.name: Split into Unit Tests per Behavior
refactoring_techniques.description: Splitting the eager test into compact independent tests following the Arrange-Act-Assert (AAA) structure.

bad_example.explanation: A single test checks 4 different methods and states. If activation breaks, the deletion check will not even be run.

good_example.explanation: The tests are isolated according to the Arrange-Act-Assert structure. Each test verifies exactly one invariant.

smells.name: Sleepy / Flaky Test
smells.summary: Using fixed pauses (Thread.sleep, setTimeout) to wait for asynchronous operations, leading to test instability.
smells.definition: An asynchronous testing smell. To wait for a background service response or an animation, the developer inserts a hard pause `Thread.sleep(2000)` or `await delay(1000)`. On a slow CI server, this pause is insufficient and the test fails; on a fast server, the test pointlessly waits for seconds, dramatically slowing down the test suite run.
symptoms: Calls to `Thread.sleep()`, `time.sleep()`, `setTimeout` directly inside test methods
Tests are intermittently 'green' and intermittently 'red' on the same commit (Flaky Tests)
Total test run time stretches to tens of minutes
root_causes: Reluctance to set up explicit polling to await predicates or subscribing to completion events
impact: Loss of team confidence in tests: developers begin ignoring CI failures ('oh, it's that flaky test again')
Slowing down the delivery pipeline

detection_metrics.hardcoded_sleep_in_tests: Presence of sleep/delay calls in test code
detection_metrics.flakiness_rate: The test changes its run outcome without changes in the code

refactoring_techniques.name: Awaitility / Polling Condition with Timeout
refactoring_techniques.description: Using condition waiting libraries (Awaitility, waitFor) with frequent polling and a strict timeout.

refactoring_techniques.name: Event-Driven Testing
refactoring_techniques.description: Waiting for the resolution of a specific promise or event in EventBus.

bad_example.explanation: If CI load is high and the operation takes 3050 ms, the test will fail with a false failure.

good_example.explanation: The test will finish immediately as soon as the email is sent (for example, in 120 ms) without delaying CI, and under overload it will wait up to 5 seconds.

smells.name: Conditional Test Logic
smells.summary: Using if/else, switch, for/while constructs inside the body of test methods.
smells.definition: A testing smell where the test method itself contains complex algorithmic logic: `if` branching and `while` loops. If there is an `if` condition in a test, this means that part of the assertions may silently not execute under a certain scenario. The test itself needs testing!
symptoms: The test contains `if ... else` branches
Asserts are hidden inside the body of a `for` loop
The test passes successfully because the `if` condition evaluated to false and not a single assert was executed
root_causes: An attempt to write one 'universal' test for different configurations
Mixing data preparation with assertion logic
impact: False positive tests (False Positives) that verify nothing
High complexity of reading the test

detection_metrics.cyclomatic_complexity_of_test: Cyclomatic complexity of the test method > 1

refactoring_techniques.name: Parameterized / Data-Driven Tests
refactoring_techniques.description: Using parameterized tests (@ParameterizedTest, test.each) instead of loops.

refactoring_techniques.name: Linearize Test
refactoring_techniques.description: Splitting if/else branches into two independent straightforward tests.

bad_example.explanation: A loop and a condition inside the test. If the `get_all_test_customers` function returns an empty list, the test will triumphantly pass.

good_example.explanation: The test has become linear, clear, and is guaranteed to execute each check in a separate isolated case.

smells.name: Test Logic in Production
smells.summary: The presence of 'if (IS_TEST_ENV)' checks or special public methods 'for testing only' in production classes.
smells.definition: A dangerous code smell where the logic of production classes is adapted to the needs of tests: conditions like `if (process.env.NODE_ENV === 'test') { bypassAuth(); }` or public methods with `@VisibleForTesting` comments appear in the code. This creates security holes and means that completely different code runs in testing than in production.
symptoms: Conditional statements `if (isTesting)` in production code
Public methods of the form `setPrivateFieldForTesting()` in domain entities
Bypassing authentication in production when a specific test header is present
root_causes: Inability to use mocks, stubs, and Dependency Injection
Difficulties in testing the private state of poorly designed classes
impact: Critical vulnerabilities in production (accidental triggering of test authorization bypass)
Tests do not guarantee the operability of actual production code

detection_metrics.test_env_checks_in_domain: Checks for test/testing environment variables in business logic

refactoring_techniques.name: Dependency Injection & Mocking
refactoring_techniques.description: Injecting mock implementations of external services via DI instead of conditional branches in prod.

refactoring_techniques.name: Test via Public Interface
refactoring_techniques.description: Testing an object exclusively through its legitimate public interface.

bad_example.explanation: The production class contains branching for tests. If this variable is accidentally set in prod, all payments will become free.

good_example.explanation: Production code is clean of test conditions. Behavior substitution is carried out via dependency injection.

smells.name: Ignored / Disabled Test Rot
smells.summary: Disabling failing tests with @Ignore, @Disabled, xit annotations instead of fixing the cause of the failure.
smells.definition: A development culture smell where a failing or unstable test is not fixed, but is marked with the `@Disabled` / `@Ignore` / `test.skip` annotation or simply commented out. Over time, such tests accumulate by the dozens, their code rots, and useful system coverage degrades.
symptoms: Multiple tests with `@Disabled("Fix later")` or `xit("...")` annotations
Disabled tests do not compile after refactoring production classes
In CI reports, the number of skipped tests exceeds 10-20%
root_causes: An urgent desire to 'fix the red build in master' before a release
Lack of a process for returning to temporarily disabled tests
impact: An illusion of test safety with an actual lack of control over critical functions
Cluttering the codebase with dead test code

refactoring_techniques.name: Fix or Delete Immediately
refactoring_techniques.description: Making a decision: either fix the test immediately, or delete it permanently.

refactoring_techniques.name: CI Policy against Skipped Tests
refactoring_techniques.description: Prohibiting merging PRs with new skipped tests in the CI pipeline.

bad_example.explanation: The test is disabled and forgotten. Real JWT validation is monitored by no one.

good_example.explanation: The test is updated and returned to the working automated verification pipeline.

smells.name: N+1 Query Problem
smells.summary: Executing a single query to fetch parent records and then N separate queries to load related data in a loop.
smells.definition: The most common and destructive performance smell when using ORMs (Hibernate, Entity Framework, Django ORM, Prisma, TypeORM). The application requests a list of N records (1 query `SELECT * FROM orders`), and then in a loop, when accessing a related entity (for example, the order customer), executes N additional queries `SELECT * FROM customers WHERE id = ?`. This leads to an avalanche of network requests to the database.
symptoms: Hundreds of identical short queries in a row with different IDs flicker in the SQL query logs
As the number of records in the table grows, endpoint response time degrades linearly (O(N))
High utilization of the DBMS connection pool
root_causes: Using Lazy Loading by default in the ORM
Lack of understanding of how the JSON serializer implicitly accesses object navigation properties
impact: Catastrophic drop in API performance under load
Overloading the DBMS with redundant round-trip network calls

detection_metrics.sql_queries_per_http_request: > 10 similar SELECT queries within a single request
detection_metrics.orm_profiler_alerts: MiniProfiler or Hibernate Query Count warnings

refactoring_techniques.name: Eager Loading (Eager loading)
refactoring_techniques.description: Using JOIN FETCH, include, select_related, or prefetch_related in the ORM.

refactoring_techniques.name: Batch Loading / Dataloader
refactoring_techniques.description: Applying the Dataloader pattern to aggregate queries by ID into a single WHERE IN operator.

bad_example.code:
# Django ORM пример:
orders = Order.objects.filter(status='COMPLETED')[:100] # 1 запрос

for order in orders:
    # На каждой итерации совершается отдельный скрытый запрос к БД!
    print(order.customer.email) # +100 запросов = 101 запрос!
bad_example.explanation: For 100 orders, 101 queries are executed against the database. At 10 000 orders, the database will simply 'go down'.

good_example.code:
# Eager Loading через select_related (делает один SQL JOIN):
orders = Order.objects.filter(status='COMPLETED').select_related('customer')[:100]

for order in orders:
    # Данные клиента уже загружены в память в первом запросе:
    print(order.customer.email) # 0 дополнительных запросов! Всего 1 запрос.
good_example.explanation: Using `select_related`, the database executes a single optimized SQL query with `INNER JOIN`, reducing network overhead to a minimum.

smells.name: In-Memory Data Filtration / Loading Whole Table
smells.name_en: In-Memory Data Filtration / Loading Whole Table
smells.summary: Dumping hundreds of thousands of records from the database into application RAM with subsequent filtering via programming language instead of SQL WHERE.
smells.definition: A severe data interaction smell. Instead of delegating filtering, sorting, or pagination to the powerful DBMS engine with its indexes, the developer executes `SELECT * FROM table`, loads gigabytes of rows into application memory, and filters them using `.filter()` or `.Where()`. This leads to OutOfMemoryError.
symptoms: Using `dbContext.Users.ToList().Where(u => ...)` in LINQ (.NET)
A sudden sharp spike in backend process RAM consumption up to gigabytes
The network pipe between the application and the database becomes clogged with the transmission of useless data
root_causes: Accidental premature invocation of terminal operations (`.ToList()`, `.all()`) before constructing filter conditions
Not knowing the difference between `IEnumerable` (in-memory) and `IQueryable` (SQL query)
impact: Server crash with an Out Of Memory (OOM) error
Slowdown of other services due to garbage collection (GC pauses)

detection_metrics.query_result_size: Loading > 5000 objects into memory in a single query without pagination
detection_metrics.memory_usage_spike: Memory leak when executing analytical queries

refactoring_techniques.name: Push Predicates to SQL (Pushing predicates to SQL)
refactoring_techniques.description: Forming conditions in WHERE prior to executing the query to the DBMS.

refactoring_techniques.name: Pagination and Streaming
refactoring_techniques.description: Mandatory use of LIMIT/OFFSET or a streaming cursor (Streaming/Cursor).

bad_example.explanation: A million records are transferred over the network from PostgreSQL to the service RAM just to filter out 10 needed rows.

good_example.explanation: Conditions are translated into an efficient `SELECT ... WHERE city = @p0 AND is_active = true LIMIT 100`. Only the required data is transferred from the database.

smells.name: God Table / Kitchen Sink Entity
smells.summary: A table in a relational database with dozens or hundreds of columns, combining disparate data from unrelated processes.
smells.definition: A database schema design smell. A table (for example, `users` or `orders`) contains 80-120 columns: profile fields, authorization parameters, credit cards, notification settings, service flags of various integrations. Most columns for a particular row are NULL, violating normalization and reducing disk I/O efficiency.
symptoms: The table has more than 40-50 columns
Most columns are nullable and populated in only 5% of rows
Any new feature from the team adds another 3-4 columns to this table
root_causes: Reluctance to create related tables and write JOINs
Architectural erosion over time
impact: Low efficiency of disk space and DBMS page cache
Frequent row locks and degradation of write speed

detection_metrics.column_count_per_table: > 40 columns in a single table of a relational DBMS
detection_metrics.null_values_percentage: > 60% NULL values across a number of columns

refactoring_techniques.name: Table Decomposition (Table decomposition)
refactoring_techniques.description: Splitting the table into several logical entities with a 1-to-1 or 1-to-many relationship.

refactoring_techniques.name: Use JSONB for Semi-Structured Attributes
refactoring_techniques.description: Moving rare and variable attributes into a structured JSONB field (PostgreSQL).

bad_example.code:
CREATE TABLE orders (
    id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
    customer_id BIGINT,
    total_price NUMERIC,
    -- Поля доставки:
    courier_name VARCHAR(100), courier_phone VARCHAR(50), car_number VARCHAR(20),
    -- Поля самовывоза:
    pickup_point_id INT, pickup_shelf_code VARCHAR(20),
    -- Поля b2b документов:
    inn VARCHAR(20), kpp VARCHAR(20), legal_address TEXT, bik VARCHAR(20),
    -- 50 других колонок...
);
bad_example.explanation: Fields for courier delivery, customer pickup, and legal entity requisites are dumped into a single table. For an individual, 70% of the columns will remain NULL.

good_example.explanation: The table is normalized. Specific data has been moved to child tables with foreign keys, saving disk space and making the schema strict.

smells.name: SQL Injection Propensity / String Concatenation
smells.summary: Forming SQL queries by concatenating strings with user data instead of using parameterized queries.
smells.definition: A critical security vulnerability and code smell (OWASP Top 10 A03: Injection). The developer concatenates variables received from the client (from a URL, form, or header) directly into the SQL query text via `f"SELECT ... WHERE name = '{user_input}'"` instead of passing parameters via placeholders (`?` or `$1`). This gives an attacker full control over the DBMS.
symptoms: String interpolation in raw SQL execution calls (`query = "SELECT ... " + input`)
Absence of parameters in `db.execute(sql)` calls
root_causes: Developer inexperience or rushing when constructing dynamic queries
Lack of understanding that an ORM does not protect when using methods like `raw()` or `executeSql()`
impact: Full database compromise: theft of all passwords, deletion of tables (DROP DATABASE)
Execution of operating system commands via xp_cmdshell / pg_read_file

detection_metrics.raw_string_formatting_in_sql: Searching for string interpolation expressions (`$`, `f""`, `%`) in SQL operations methods

refactoring_techniques.name: Use Parameterized Queries / Prepared Statements
refactoring_techniques.description: Passing values strictly via parameters and prepared queries.

refactoring_techniques.name: Use Safe Query Builders
refactoring_techniques.description: Using query builders (Knex, SQLAlchemy Core, jOOQ) that eliminate concatenation.

bad_example.explanation: By passing `category_id = "1' OR '1'='1"`, an attacker will retrieve all hidden products or delete data.

good_example.explanation: Data is passed separately from the command body. The DBMS compiles the query plan in advance and treats the parameter strictly as a data string, eliminating injection.

smells.name: Unindexed Foreign Keys and Filter Fields
smells.name_en: Unindexed Foreign Keys and Filter Fields
smells.summary: Foreign Keys and frequently filtered fields are not covered by B-Tree indexes, causing a Full Table Scan.
smells.definition: A relational database schema design smell (especially in PostgreSQL and Oracle, which unlike MySQL InnoDB do not create indexes on FKs automatically). When performing a JOIN or deleting a parent record, the DBMS is forced to scan the entire child table (Seq Scan / Table Scan), locking the table and causing multi-second delays.
symptoms: The `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` query plan shows `Seq Scan` on a million-row table when executing a JOIN
The operation `DELETE FROM customers WHERE id = 1` unexpectedly hangs for several seconds
High disk I/O on the database server
root_causes: False assumption that `REFERENCES` automatically creates an index in any DBMS
Lack of slow query monitoring (`pg_stat_statements`)
impact: Severe slowdowns during table join operations and cascade deletions
Performance degradation as data volume grows

detection_metrics.unindexed_fk_ratio: Presence of foreign key columns without a corresponding B-tree index

refactoring_techniques.name: Add Explicit Index on Foreign Keys
refactoring_techniques.description: Creating indexes on all foreign key columns and frequent WHERE filter fields.

bad_example.code:
CREATE TABLE order_items (
    id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    -- Внешний ключ объявлен, но индекса НЕТ в PostgreSQL!
    order_id BIGINT REFERENCES orders(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    product_id BIGINT REFERENCES products(id),
    quantity INT
);
bad_example.explanation: When deleting an order from the `orders` table, PostgreSQL will scan the entire multi-million row `order_items` table with sequential disk reads.

good_example.explanation: The created indexes provide instant lookup of related order items across the binary tree in O(log N).

smells.name: Hardcoded Credentials / API Keys
smells.summary: Storing passwords, private keys, JWT secrets, and API tokens directly in the repository source code.
smells.definition: A critical security vulnerability (OWASP Top 10 A07: Identification and Authentication Failures). The developer inserts a private AWS access token, database password, or secret JWT signing key directly into a string constant in the code. When publishing the repository to GitHub/GitLab, the secret instantly enters leak scanner databases and is used by attackers to breach the infrastructure.
symptoms: Presence of strings like `apiKey = "AIzaSy..."` or `password = "SuperSecret123!"` in the source code
Warnings from secret scanning systems (Gitleaks, TruffleHog, GitHub Secret Scanning)
root_causes: Rapid prototyping followed by forgetting to move secrets to secure storage
Lack of understanding that Git history preserves deleted lines forever
impact: Instant compromise of cloud infrastructure, databases, and payment accounts
Huge financial and reputational losses

detection_metrics.high_entropy_strings: Detection of strings with high entropy characteristic of RSA/JWT/API keys
detection_metrics.git_secret_scanning_hits: Gitleaks triggers in the pre-commit pipeline

refactoring_techniques.name: Externalize Secrets to Secret Manager
refactoring_techniques.description: Moving secrets to HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, or environment variables.

refactoring_techniques.name: Revoke and Rotate Compromised Keys
refactoring_techniques.description: Immediate revocation of the compromised key and its complete rotation.

bad_example.explanation: AWS secret keys are hardcoded into the source code. If the repository leaks, attackers will gain full control over cloud storage.

good_example.explanation: Secrets are not stored in the repository, but are injected at the deployment stage via a secure environment or Secret Manager.

smells.name: Resource Leak / Unclosed Handles
smells.summary: Opening file descriptors, sockets, or DB connections without guaranteed closure in finally / using / with blocks.
smells.definition: A systems programming smell. The program acquires an operating system system resource (file descriptor, TCP socket, DB connection pool connection, graphics context) and fails to release it when an error occurs. Over time, the operating system exhausts the open file limit (`Too many open files`), and the service crashes.
symptoms: Error `EMFILE: too many open files` or `SocketException: No buffer space available`
Exhaustion of the DB connection pool under load ('Connection pool timeout')
Files on disk remain locked and cannot be deleted until the process is restarted
root_causes: Manual closing with `.close()` at the end of a function without a `finally` block (on any exception close is not called)
Lack of knowledge of automatic resource management constructs (`using` in C#, `try-with-resources` in Java, `with` in Python)
impact: Server crash when OS file descriptors are exhausted
Database crash due to hanging zombie connections

detection_metrics.unmanaged_resources_without_cleanup: Calls to open/connect without using, try-with-resources, or with

refactoring_techniques.name: Use RAII / Try-with-resources / Using / With
refactoring_techniques.description: Wrapping resource handling in language constructs for guaranteed release.

bad_example.code:
def process_data_file(filepath: str) -> str:
    # ОШИБКА: если json.load упадет с ошибкой, файл останется открытым в ОС навсегда!
    f = open(filepath, 'r')
    data = json.load(f)
    f.close()
    return data['status']
bad_example.explanation: In the event of a syntax error in the JSON, the `f.close()` call will never execute, leading to a file descriptor leak.

good_example.code:
def process_data_file(filepath: str) -> str:
    # Менеджер контекста 'with' гарантированно закроет файл даже при падении:
    with open(filepath, 'r') as f:
        data = json.load(f)
        return data['status']
good_example.explanation: The `with` construct guarantees that the descriptor close method is called under any outcome, eliminating the leak of OS resources.

smells.name: Sensitive Data Exposure in Logs
smells.summary: Writing passwords, bank card numbers (PAN), authorization tokens, and personal data (PII) to logs.
smells.definition: A serious violation of security and compliance requirements (GDPR, 152-FZ, PCI-DSS). Developers output the full request object to logs `logger.info("Registering user: " + JSON.stringify(req.body))`, resulting in plaintext passwords and credit card data settling in centralized log storages (Elasticsearch, Datadog) accessible to a wide audience.
symptoms: User passwords can be found in Kibana / Grafana Loki by searching for the word `"password"`
Logging the `Authorization: Bearer ...` header without masking
Complaints from security auditors regarding PCI-DSS standards
root_causes: Mindless logging of DTOs and entire objects for the sake of quick debugging
Absence of masking filters (Redaction Filters) in the logger configuration
impact: Theft of user accounts by employees with access to logs
Huge regulatory fines for personal data leakage

refactoring_techniques.name: Data Masking / Redaction Filter
refactoring_techniques.description: Introducing automatic masking of sensitive fields in the logger (replacement with `***`).

refactoring_techniques.name: Log Only Business Identifiers
refactoring_techniques.description: Logging only identifiers (User ID, Order ID) instead of the entire object.

bad_example.explanation: The user's plaintext password enters the log index and becomes accessible to any engineer or tech support.

good_example.explanation: Only the user identifier is passed to the logs. Sensitive data (passwords, tokens) are excluded from the logs.

smells.name: Disabled Certificate Validation / Insecure TLS
smells.summary: Disabling SSL certificate validation (rejectUnauthorized: false, check_hostname=False), opening the door to Man-in-the-Middle attacks.
smells.definition: A critical security vulnerability smell. Facing a 'self-signed certificate' error during local development, a developer disables the TLS/SSL trust chain check (for example, `ServerCertificateCustomValidationCallback = HttpClientHandler.DangerousAcceptAnyServerCertificateValidator` or `NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED = '0'`). If this flag reaches production, any attacker on the local network can intercept and decrypt all encrypted traffic (MitM).
symptoms: Presence of `NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED = '0'` in the code
Use of `DangerousAcceptAnyServerCertificateValidator` in C#
`verify=False` in calls to the `requests` library in Python
root_causes: The desire to quickly bypass issues with corporate proxies or local self-signed certificates
Reluctance to properly add a root certificate (CA) to the OS trusted store
impact: Complete vulnerability to Man-in-the-Middle attacks: interception of passwords, tokens, and tampering with API responses

detection_metrics.tls_reject_unauthorized_false: Searching for settings that disable SSL validation in network clients

refactoring_techniques.name: Install Self-Signed CA into Trust Store
refactoring_techniques.description: Installing a test root certificate into the trusted system store.

refactoring_techniques.name: Strict TLS Enforcement
refactoring_techniques.description: Complete ban on insecure connections in production code.

bad_example.explanation: The `verify=False` flag allows any intermediate router or Wi-Fi hotspot to intercept and modify banking data.

good_example.explanation: SSL validation is 100% enabled. For internal servers, the path to a trusted corporate CA is provided.

smells.name: Prop Drilling
smells.summary: Passing props through 4-6 intermediate components that do not need this data, for the sake of delivering it to a deeply nested child component.
smells.definition: A component design smell in frontend frameworks (React, Vue, Svelte). To pass data (for example, `theme`, `currentUser`, or an `onLogout` callback) from a parent container to a deeply nested button, the developer is forced to pass this parameter through a dozen intermediate components (`Page` -> `Layout` -> `Header` -> `NavBar` -> `UserMenu` -> `LogoutButton`).
symptoms: Intermediate components have bloated Props interfaces consisting of fields that they do not use themselves
Changing a prop's type requires edits across all 6 transit components
Difficulty in reusing intermediate components in a different context
root_causes: Ignoring context mechanisms (React Context, Vue Provide/Inject)
Lack of knowledge of the component composition pattern (Component Composition / Inversion of Control)
impact: Excessive coupling of the entire component tree
Unnecessary re-renders of intermediate components

detection_metrics.prop_drilling_depth: Passing the same prop through >= 3 levels of component nesting without using it

refactoring_techniques.name: Use React Context / State Management Store
refactoring_techniques.description: Providing data via Context or a global state manager (Zustand, Redux Toolkit, Pinia).

refactoring_techniques.name: Component Composition (Slots / Children)
refactoring_techniques.description: Passing a ready instantiated child element via the `children` prop.

bad_example.explanation: The `Header` and `Navigation` components simply relay `currentUser` and `onLogout` further down, polluting their API.

good_example.explanation: The intermediate component is freed from pass-through parameters. The target element reads data directly from context.

smells.name: Direct DOM Manipulation in Reactive Frameworks
smells.name_en: Direct DOM Manipulation in Reactive Frameworks
smells.summary: Using document.getElementById or direct DOM tree mutations bypassing the framework's reactive Virtual DOM.
smells.definition: A frontend development smell in declarative frameworks (React, Vue, Angular). The developer attempts to change an element's class, hide a block, or insert text via imperative calls such as `document.querySelector('#modal').classList.add('open')` instead of managing state (`isOpen = true`). This breaks consistency between the Virtual DOM and the real DOM, leading to visual artifacts and desynchronization of the interface.
symptoms: Calls to `document.getElementById`, `window.document`, `$('.class')` inside React/Vue components
An element disappears or resets its styles on the next render of the component
Inability to render the component on the server side (Server-Side Rendering / SSR fails due to missing `document`)
root_causes: Habits from the jQuery library era
Misunderstanding the declarative nature of modern UI libraries
impact: Desynchronization between application state and the user's actual screen
SSR crashes (Next.js / Nuxt) with `ReferenceError: document is not defined` errors

detection_metrics.direct_dom_calls_count: Using native DOM API methods in component code without `useRef`

refactoring_techniques.name: State-Driven Declarative Rendering
refactoring_techniques.description: Controlling element display exclusively via state (useState/ref).

refactoring_techniques.name: Use Framework Refs
refactoring_techniques.description: Using `useRef` in React exclusively for focusing or measuring geometry.

bad_example.explanation: Direct style mutation via `getElementById`. On any rerender of the parent component, the banner will reappear because React is unaware of it being hidden.

good_example.explanation: Declarative control via local `useState` state. The framework fully controls the rendering and lifecycle of the DOM.

smells.name: Giant Component / God Component
smells.summary: A single component file contains more than 500 lines, mixing business logic, API requests, complex styles, and dozens of markup elements.
smells.definition: The frontend counterpart to the Large Class / God Object smell. A page or form component expands to enormous proportions: it declares 20 `useState` hooks, 10 `useEffect` hooks, direct network `fetch` calls, form validation, modal windows, and hundreds of lines of JSX markup. Such a component is impossible to understand, and any change leads to slow rendering of the entire screen.
symptoms: Component file contains over 400-600 lines of code
More than 8 state hooks (`useState` / `useReducer`) in a single component
Slow interface responsiveness (Laggy Input) due to heavy re-rendering of the entire component on every keystroke
root_causes: Incremental feature buildup without decomposition into subcomponents
Mixing presentation (UI) and business logic in a single file
impact: Sharp drop in page rendering performance
Inability to reuse individual UI blocks

detection_metrics.component_loc: > 300 lines of code in a single component file

refactoring_techniques.name: Custom Hooks Extraction
refactoring_techniques.description: Extracting data loading logic and state management into custom hooks (for example, `useOrderForm`).

refactoring_techniques.name: Sub-component Decomposition
refactoring_techniques.description: Decomposing markup into small atomic components (OrderItem, OrderSummary, ShippingSection).

bad_example.explanation: The component is overloaded with state and logic, violating SRP and slowing down the browser.

good_example.explanation: The component has become a concise orchestrator. Logic is moved to the `useCheckoutFlow` hook, and the interface is divided into independent subcomponents.

smells.name: Zombie Subscriptions / Unsubscribed Observers
smells.summary: Subscribing to window events (addEventListener, setInterval, WebSocket) inside hooks without a cleanup function on unmount.
smells.definition: A dangerous code smell in frontend applications. Inside a `useEffect` hook or lifecycle hook, a global listener `window.addEventListener('resize', handler)` is attached or a `setInterval` timer is started, but the cleanup function (`return () => cleanup()`) is omitted. With each navigation between pages by the user, a new duplicate listener is created, leaking memory and invoking handlers of already destroyed components.
symptoms: Constant growth in browser tab RAM consumption (Memory Leak)
A callback executes 10 times instead of 1 on a single click or window resize
Console warning: 'Can't perform a React state update on an unmounted component'
root_causes: Forgetting to return a cleanup function from the `useEffect` hook
Losing the handler reference due to creating an anonymous arrow function
impact: Browser tab sluggishness and freezing of the client's device
Unpredictable side effects from zombie components

detection_metrics.use_effect_without_cleanup: Presence of addEventListener/setInterval in useEffect without a paired remove/clearInterval in return

refactoring_techniques.name: Always Return Cleanup Function
refactoring_techniques.description: Guaranteed unsubscription from all data sources in the hook's returned function.

refactoring_techniques.name: Use AbortController for Async Fetch
refactoring_techniques.description: Cancelling network requests via AbortSignal upon component unmounting.

bad_example.explanation: When the component is reopened, the old scroll handler remains in memory forever, retaining the component's closure.

good_example.explanation: The hook returns a cleanup function that cleanly detaches the event handler when the component is destroyed.

smells.name: Duplicated Derived State
smells.summary: Storing values in useState that can be easily computed on the fly from existing props or state.
smells.definition: Reactive state smell. A developer introduces a separate `useState` for data that is derived from other data (for example, `const [fullName, setFullName] = useState()` when `firstName` and `lastName` exist, or `const [filteredList, setFilteredList] = useState()` when `list` and `searchQuery` exist). As a result, they have to synchronize them through complex `useEffect` chains, which leads to data desynchronization and bugs.
symptoms: `useEffect` hooks that merely call `setDerivedState(calculate(prop))`
The user changes the first name, and the last name or full name updates with a one-frame delay (Render Glitch)
Multiple sources of truth (Single Source of Truth is violated) for the same value
root_causes: Lack of understanding that rendering in React is a pure function of props and state
A false fear of performance degradation caused by simple calculations during render
impact: UI desynchronization and the emergence of hard-to-catch state bugs
Double rendering of components (first updating the prop, then firing the effect and updating derived state)

detection_metrics.use_effect_state_sync_pattern: Using useEffect exclusively to move data into an adjacent useState

refactoring_techniques.name: Compute during Render (Computation during render)
refactoring_techniques.description: Replacing useState and useEffect with a regular constant in the function body.

refactoring_techniques.name: Use useMemo for Expensive Computations
refactoring_techniques.description: Wrapping truly expensive calculations (hundreds of thousands of elements) in a useMemo hook.

bad_example.explanation: Redundant `useState` and redundant `useEffect`. When the name changes, the component will first display the old `fullName`, and only after the effect fires will it re-render with the new one.

good_example.explanation: The value is computed instantly during execution of the render function. There is a single source of truth, and redundant renders are absent.
